utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution rested its case on Tuesday and submits that there is sufficient to proceed with the case as alleged in the indictment against the accused, Naser Oric. In its submission yesterday, the Defence did not address the nucleus of evidence adduced. The case is to show that the accused Naser Oric has been a commander of the Srebrenica armed forces and the subregion in the period 1992, 1993, of the indictment and that under his command, responsibility, crimes has been committed such as wanton destruction of villages and plunder of property related to five attacks and killings and cruel treatments of prisoners, as well as that he planned, instigated, ordered or aided and abetted wanton destruction and plunder related to three of the five attacks mentioned. The Prosecution's evidence was not, as pleaded in the indictment, accusations that civilians steal food to feed themselves, as suggested by the Defence yesterday. The Prosecution's case is not a selective criminal forum to judge cases to please political interest. The Prosecution submits that justice should be done in this case and other cases irrespective of the religious, ethnic, or national background of the victims or the accused. These are the considerations that drive the Prosecution case against Naser Oric. The result of war crimes is the suffering. Your Honours, it should be clear that civilians suffer from the wanton destructions of their homes and the plunder of their properties. Those are great losses to overcome. Murder and cruel treatment of detainees are a serious war crime. Each of these forms of suffering are prohibited by national criminal codes, international treaties, and customary law. Other atrocities committed in Srebrenica during the very armed conflict that is the background of the present case have been investigated and prosecuted by this Prosecutor and adjudicated by your fellow trial and appeal chambers. Convictions were the result of it. The present case brings to justice the crimes committed against Bosnian Serbs in Srebrenica and surrounding municipalities in 1992 and 1993. For that, Your Honours, the evidence clearly demonstrate that Naser Oric has a case to answer. I give now the floor for the second chapter to Ms. Patricia Sellers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, learned counsel. Your Honours, my submissions today will be brief and right to the point. It will be a response to the submission by the Defence as it relates to counts 1 and 2. Yesterday, the Defence conceded the crime base that Dragutin Kukic had been killed in the prison in Srebrenica. They also conceded that he had been killed by a man named Kemo and that he had been beaten to death. What the Defence raises was a question of mens rea of the crime of murder. Now, they insist, under the Kupreskic standard that that death had to be premeditated, intentional. Your Honours, I will just briefly state that the Kupreskic standard, if you take that standard, although there are others that have superseded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will dispense you from having to deal with whether we ought to take as one of the requirements premeditation. I can assure you we are not going to take it now, neither now nor later nor ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour then might I just quickly move on to say that the mens rea has been not only completed by the acts of Kemo but substantiated by the testimony of Mr. Nedjeljko Radic who he himself received beatings with the same pieces of wood that he stated measures 80 centimetres. The beatings that were inflicted upon him caused his ribs to be broken, caused him severe pain. Whether asked was the beating administered to Mr. Kukic of the same force or greater, he said it was even greater. Your Honour, I believe that the mens rea, whether it's intentional or this person was caused serious grievous bodily harm has been completed. I will now move on to the next part of my arguments, if you please, and that is the question of subordination. The Defence has raised the issue that given that the crime has been committed, given that Kemo did kill Mr. Kukic, that the Prosecution's evidence does not show that Kemo was a subordinate. And in order to substantiate that Kemo was not a subordinate, the Defence went to the testimony of Prosecution Witness Hakija Meholjic and it said that Mr. Meholjic didn't know if Kemo was a soldier, wasn't quite certain or if he was, who was his commander. Now, the quote that the Defence showed us yesterday was incomplete. If one had looked at that quote in its larger sense a bit more carefully, it was clear that Mr. Meholjic said, "I did not have the possibility to learn about any of the appointments because nobody was duty bound to inform me about that. At the end of the war, Mandzo Mrki whose first name was Ibrahim, if I'm not mistaken, I'm sure." This was his response as to who was the commander of Kemo. Further up in that same section, he says, "I don't know if he belonged to anybody, he belonged to the Potocari unit." So we have the Potocari unit, we have Ibrahim Mandzic, Mrki Mandzo, but we have more than that on the record, Your Honours. I'm certain that you're familiar by this time with P80. P80 is a document that both the Defence and the Prosecution have shown witnesses, have placed into evidence, and have substanture [phoen] to a large part. Now, without entering into any discussion about authenticity or credibility, but about what is clearly written on the document, I would invite you to look at P80. On the first page, it talks about the formation structure of the Srebrenica OS armed forces. Section 1, section 1 talks about the territorial organisation of Potocari. If one were to go down merely three lines, we have the Pale company. Kemo is often referred to as Kemo from Pale. Now, the Pale company as part of the Potocari TO was commanded by Mirzet Halilovic and it's also been commanded by Smazo Mandzic [phoen]. If one goes a bit further down in that first section, I would say four lines from the bottom of the first section, it also says the Budak company. Now, you can look at Sanctions and you can see that the Budak company with 139 conscripts was commanded by Ibrahim Mandzic. There is testimony on the record from Mr. Nedjeljko Radic, our eyewitness to the murder that says that Kemo was in uniform. As one goes through the document of P80, it is certain, it is clear, that the Potocari TO remains under the command of Naser Oric throughout the relevant time period, not only of this indictment but the relevant time period of the murder of Mr. Dragutin Kukic, and I would just briefly refer you to page 4 of P80, the same document, midway through the page. Once again we have the Potocari Brigade and under it the Pale battalion based in Pale. If one went to other documents that we have used, for example, P9, again the organisation of the Srebrenica forces and the commander orders the formation of a brigade, Potocari Brigade, will be composed of battalion from Pale. Now, the Defence also said, well, it's an independent battalion, a brigade. It's one that doesn't come under Naser Oric. And the document that they had used last week to show Prosecution witness General Delic, if you look through it carefully, there is not one mention that the Pale battalion or Potocari was independent. But the Prosecution would say that there is evidence on the record that makes us understand that this point is minutiae. Again looking at P80, one sees through the progression of the development of the companies and the battalions under the Srebrenica armed forces, that there are often independent battalions. I would ask you to look at page 6 of P80 where, under numbers 4, 5, 6, and 7, we have the independent Srebrenica Battalion, the independent Sikirici Battalion, the Independent Belidj [phoen] Battalion, the Independent Osmace Battalion, all subordinated to the Srebrenica armed forces, in other words subordinated to Naser Oric. So, Your Honours, we do have the mens rea, we do have a subordinate, and then the Defence has asked us to really consider the question, did Naser Oric have specific information that one of his subordinates committed a crime? And therefore, he should be prompted to punish the crime. Now, I would direct the Trial Chamber's attention to the standard set out for inquiry notice under the Blaskic appeals decision. It's not specific information. If you would permit me to read the more correct standard from what I would say right now is our Tribunal's highest authority, it asks whether a superior has only information that is available to him. They say, "A superior will be criminally liable, criminally responsible, through the principles of superior responsibility only if information was available to him which would have put him on notice of offences committed by subordinates." It's not specific information. And without belabouring the point, I think Your Honours are familiar with the Celebici decision which basically is the first time that we look at this concept of inquiry notice. The Celebici appeals decision, as confirmed by the Blaskic appeals decision, says that you have to look at a breadth of information. Among the information could be the character of the perpetrator. Now, there has been substantial evidence on the record about the character of Kemo. There has not been one person who has come and not said that this was a violent man. We have evidence on the record of his participation in attacks where mutilations, bodily mutilations have occurred. We have other evidence on the record that speaks about Kemo being out of control. That is information available to a commander in terms of having a subordinate like that near prisoners of war, persons hors de combat or detainees who at a minimum are to get humane treatment. But I would ask Your Honours, even given the well known reputation of the character traits of Kemo, a violent erratic person, that Mr. Oric had other information. And that information was available to him. First of all, he goes to the detention centre and inquires about the death of Dragutin Kukic. He knows the person is dead. The response he gets from huddled prisoners is the heart attack. One could say, well he's alerted to the fact that he has lost a prisoner of war, someone who could have been valuable to be exchanged because those prisoners of war were held for exchange purposes. And he could have inquired, where is the body? Maybe I could exchange the body for Muslim soldiers alive or dead. But he receives other information. He's informed by October 14th that Mirsad Halilovic has beaten a prisoner to death. Now, Mirsad Halilovic is the chief of police. He's beaten a prisoner to death. Naser Oric knows who the prisoners are. And he know that is a prisoner has died in prison. He could have asked those very same prisoners, who were still present on October 14th, as other commanders have, asked the prisoners and asked the rest of his personnel, his subordinates in the military police, what happened? It appears that Misad Halilovic had beaten a prisoner to death. The story would have come out, no it wasn't Mirzet Halilovic, it was Kemo who beat the prisoner to death. There was inquiry notice, information available to him upon which he could have acted. And the information would have led him to the real perpetrator of the crime. It was committed not by his subordinate, Mirzet Halilovic but by his subordinate Kemo. Now, returning just very briefly to this uncontrollable impulsive Kemo. One has to go back to the quote of Hakija Meholjic because it said in reference to Kemo, "He did cause problems, but when I appeared, I being Hakija, all the problems stopped. He was not as brave as one may have believed." And when one looks at the interview by Naser Oric and his comments on Kemo, he said "he really wasn't that good of a fighter, a little average." Kemo is a subordinate, could have been controlled, should have been punished for the death of Dragutin Kukic. Your Honours, I will now move on to cruel treatment. The Defence again raised the issue on cruel treatment about well, who were the people who committed the cruel treatment and I at this point in time am talking about the first group of prisoners who came from September 24th, 25th, after the Podrinje attack, and also Mr. Zikic who came after the Fakovici attack, until they were released on October 16th. So let's look at the subordinate relationship to the beatings during that first period. We've already established that Kemo was a subordinate. Nedjeljko Radic says that Kemo was there every time the beatings were administered, subordinate present administering the beatings. The cruel beatings that the Defence has conceded occurred. Who else was there? Mrki. Mrki in a uniform. Mr. Nedjeljko Radic came back on the second day of his testimony and said "Yes, I remember the Mrki, the uniform. He had a uniform like Naser Oric, the one with the lilies, the emblems on it. Yes he was in the room where the beatings always took place." Who else beat the prisoners? Well, I would like the Trial Chamber to look at a very brief selection of one of our exhibits, a video, that will talk about another person who beat the prisoners. I believe we are having a problem with the sound, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't hear any sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Neither can I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's probably the sound level. I don't know. Before when this happened, it was the sound level which needed adjustment. Perhaps let's -- because I don't want this to deprive us of precious time, Ms. Sellers. If you can just say it would this person is, we all know but I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours and I will just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And which person does he refer to? That should be enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, on this clip, the person we see has been identified as one of the prisoners, Veselin Sarac [phoen]. He will state on this clip that he was beaten by Mirsad Halilovic, the chief of police, subordinate to Naser Oric. On the clip he will also state that he was beaten, kicked with boots, during the interrogation in the police station which served as the police prison. Subordinate of Naser Oric inflicting cruel treatment. Now, who were the other people that inflicted cruel treatment, often described as soldiers, persons coming in. I would ask Your Honours to give another consideration, that whoever the physical perpetrators were, beyond the subordinates that we've identified including a subordinate named Beli [phoen] who transferred one of the prisoners to the prison from the Podravanje attack, who Mr. Zikic says, "I don't know what Beli had against me." Maybe someone in his family was injured, or harmed or killed in Fakovici, but Beli, that soldier, a subordinate of Naser Oric, would come to the jail cell and beat him through the bars. But Your Honours, the other consideration is where are the beatings taking place? We are in the prison of the military police. Now there has been a lot of testimony concerning the military police and I would just like to remind Your Honours that it is clear not only from the testimony of Mr. Bogilovic, the military police were under who, they were under Naser Oric, when Mirsad Halilovic was transferred under the supervision of Mr. Bogilovic, a civilian police person, "Well, did the whole military police force go with you?" "No, no, no. I only had Mirsad Halilovic." The military police remained under the control of the army subordinated to Naser Oric. But we could look at the documents, we could go back to P4 and P4 dates from the 15th of June and what it says is at the VP, the military police, the organisation is to be carried out by Mirsad Halilovic, confirmed by Mr. Bogilovic, confirmed within the interview with Mr. Oric. If one would go to P100 once again we see a decision was made to form wartime military police, Mirsad Halilovic was appointed the commander of this unit. And this is sent to Sarajevo and Tuzla informing them that under the TO Staff of Srebrenica, Mirsad Halilovic would form a military police unit. And if we went right past the exchange date of this first group of prisoners and looked at P5, we have an order coming from Naser Oric ordering the military police to carry out an investigation in Krusev Do pursuant to one of the orders of the War Presidency. Now, Mr. Bogilovic testified to that and stated that, yes, Naser Oric was ordering the military police. He still had superior responsibility via his command of the military police throughout the month of October when the crimes occurred. Now, my last point that I will addressing you with concerns inquiry notice of the cruel treatment. Mr. Oric didn't know they were being beaten up. He didn't know that cruel treatment was inflicted. First of all we are led to believe that it wasn't Mr. Oric who came to the prison, who came and saw the prisoners in the jail cell. He didn't see Mr. Radic, Mr. Veselin Saric, he didn't see Mr. Zikic, he really wasn't there and couldn't see Mr. Brankovic. The testimony is contrary to that supposition. How do we know that Naser Oric came? Well, it's not a question of these little important features, the beard, not the beard. Veselin Saric knew Naser Oric from before the war. And told the other prisoners it's Naser Oric. So we know that the Naser Oric was present at the prison and saw these prisoners, but inquiry notice. Okay, now, could he really see anyone having blood coming out of their mouth, being broken, being stooped? He had several opportunities. Not only have we been informed via testimony that the prison cell was quite small. If one could not see clearly, one could smell, one could see the forms huddled against the floor trying to lean against the wall. But we have more than that. Veselin Saric is taken out of the cell several times, not just for interrogation but to speak via communication, Motorola or radio, group 2 to negotiate an exchange, taken out of the cell into another room next to Naser Oric. It's a matter of fact, during that conversation, Veselin Saric is made to say, "Oh, yes, I'm fine, they haven't beaten me." Nedjeljko Radic has already informed us that by that time they've been beaten often, continuously and severely. That's information available to Naser Oric. But if we put that aside, Naser Oric sees them all together on another occasion, takes them out of the cell, and is in the room with the stove. This is just two days before they are exchanged. That means this is the accumulation of all the beating, all of the cruel treatment that they have been subjected to. And he sits and he talks to them because a relative of his has been killed during the war. He clearly sees them and he is in the company of Kemo and Mrki and Mr. Oric strikes Veselin Saric, angry that he won't say that he knows who Akif Ustic is. As a matter of fact, Veselin Saric talks about that. If we could just go to this video clip. If the sound is working now, it would be the second one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the point is almost too obvious. Naser Oric sees the men beaten, broken, the day before they are exchanged. He himself administers a blow. He has the information that is available to him that these men are being beaten. The cruel treatment committed by his subordinates was never acted upon by Naser Oric. Naser Oric has a case to answer, in terms of the cruel treatment, and of the murders that relate to that relevant time period in count 1 and 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers. I now call upon Mr. Di Fazio to deal with --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanne Richardson will now finish counts 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I would like to pick up from where co-counsel Mrs. Sellers left off with respect to the relationship Naser Oric had to the military police and others who were involved with the prisoners that were kept in Srebrenica during the period of 1993. After the dismissal of Mirsad Halilovic, we have essentially a restructuring of the military police. I would invite you to look at Prosecution's Exhibit P11, which is a decision by the Chief of Staff of the OS, and it specifically refers to the reorganisation. It describes what the military police should now be formulated, with respect to battalions and brigades. It also speaks to the fact that in the Srebrenica town itself, the military police would have a platoon consisting of three squads with nine members each. The next exhibit confirms, Prosecution Exhibit 9, confirms in fact that the battalions, as it pertained to the armed forces, were indeed very detailed and organised, listing various areas. And this is an order that was signed by Naser Oric. I invite you to take a look at Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the number of this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: P9. The first exhibit I referred to was P11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would invite to you look at the next exhibit, Prosecution's Exhibit number 12, again from the OS staff, Osman Osmanovic, the chief. And this is a decision which essentially now names Akif Kurtic [phoen] as the military police commander, and as well as stating that he is authorised to make independent decisions with respect to the military police. It also states that any changes must be reported to or made known to the OS staff and the reasons regarding any dismissals, et cetera. I should also point out that Akif Kurtic was not in now to the armed forces of Srebrenica. He had been a member of the Territorial Defence staff prior. Next, Prosecution's Exhibit 38. I also want to point out that in Prosecution's Exhibit P11, the military police is referred to as the Srebrenica armed forces military police, the OS, excuse me, military police. No indication that there are in any way connected to Tuzla or Sarajevo but in fact belongs to Srebrenica armed forces. Prosecution's Exhibit 38 essentially spells out one of the duties of the military police, stating that any disobedience, referring to the last sentence, any disobedience on the part of the soldiers must be reported to the military police section commander, again confirming Prosecution Exhibit P11 regarding the battalions and the manner in which the military police was reorganised. With respect to some of these duties, I invite Your Honours to review Prosecution Exhibit P15 which spells out the patrol order detailing the times that they are supposed to be patrolling, and this is signed by the military commander Akif Kurtic. The second page of that document is telling with respect to their obligations regarding the prisoners, stating "at 1300 hours we took two prisoners of war to the OS Staff for interviewing." Incidentally, I should note with respect to this document, various police officers that are named in this document also appear in the military log, Prosecution's Exhibit P458, which we refer to and used during the Prosecution's case. Page 4 of this same document details prisoners that were brought, prisoners of war that were brought from Cerska by Ibrahim Mandza, and you may recall a number of witnesses talked about Mandza and the fact that he was involved in the exchange announcing to them in the prison that they were about to be exchanged, accompanying them to the exchange. The persons listed, I will get to when I talk about what was testified to by the witnesses. Page 7 of this report also details and confirms an obligation that the police -- the military police had with respect to the prisoners. Towards the middle of the page it states, the duty officer in the staff was Esad Salihovic [phoen] and Harim [phoen] Hasanovic. Was the duty officer in the hospital with the wounded prisoner instead of Rifat Ibric [phoen]. And again, I invite you to compare the names that appear in this report with those that appear in the military log. There will be no doubt that in fact the military police was operating in Srebrenica and not only was -- were they operating, they had a specific obligation with respect to the prisoners. Again, Prosecution Exhibit P13 talks about another obligation of the military police, with respect to the armed forces. This is an order from Naser Oric, all members of the Srebrenica -- all members of the armed forces of Srebrenica, and he listed the various areas, are to be transferred from their home units to the unit commander, to the unit commanded by Desanovic Hasim [phoen]. This order is to be executed immediately and those who fail to comply must be reported to the military police. Again showing the direct link to Naser Oric, his communications with the military police, and their obligations in Srebrenica. Now, Your Honour, I would like to turn to the witnesses who testified in this case, the witnesses who testified about their detention in the police station in 1993 as well as in the prison. I first would like to refer you to Ilija Ivanovic, whom you may remember testified at length about the fact that he was in police station brought into the police station by soldiers, and that during that period of time that he was in the police station, he was beaten and kicked, he banged his head on the radiator. He remembered that very well. He was rendered unconscious, and other persons who were with him during that period of time were beaten as well, and he named them, and those were Ratko Nikolic, Kostadin, which is Kostadin Popovic, Mile Trifunovic, and Bogdan, he also named. He also talked about the fact that he was interrogated and he believed at the time that he was interrogated that he was speaking with a judge and in the presence of that person, who he believed was a judge, were two soldiers and he was also threatened and this man told him he was going to skin him and put salt in his wounds. He was returned to the cell where the beatings of not only Mr. Ivanovic but of all the other prisoners who were there resumed with metal rods, with rifle butts, with wooden bats, whatever they could get their hands on, Your Honour. And I will turn to -- at the end of my submission or just before I get to the end, refer you to various documents which confirms what he testified to the Court about his interrogation. And throughout the testimony of the various witnesses that appeared, they all confirmed that they were interrogated. And we showed documents, some of which we will refer to today, those -- the interrogation was primarily conducted by Hamid Salihovic, the head of security and intelligence, and he was also, of course, a member of the OS Staff. And just in brief, you may recall that in fact that there was some sort of commission for an exchange with the enemy that he assessed them, he made a determination, he made a recommendation, and I will get to that in a moment. Getting back to Mr. Ivanovic, he testified that he had been taken to the hospital at a later point where he was kept with Rado Pejic and others. But prior to being taken to the hospital, he testified that he was transferred from the police station to the prison, where other prisoners were brought in. Those other prisoners, namely Branko Sekulic, Jakov Djukic, Dragan Ilic, Rade Pejic, and a female, Andja. He recalls there was a total of 14 prisoners in all. He also recalls that there it was a boy and a girl who you may recall testified. The boy referred to as Branko, who is Branimir Mitrovic [phoen] and Svetlana Trifunovic whose grandfather Milo Trifunovic was in the prison as well. And as I said before, I will get to those documents which confirms the fact that these prisoners were brought in from Cerska and if fact the Prosecution's exhibit that I just referred to showing the reports from the police officer details the same names that I just referred to from Cerska. Now, Mr. Ivanovic testified that during the time this he was in prison where they were beaten on a daily basis by guards, by other people who would be let in by the guards, he testified that they were beaten all the time, and he also testified that there was this one soldier who was a guard who did not beat them and, interestingly enough, this person said to him that "Listen, Chetnik," I'm quoting from the transcript, "Listen Chetnik, even if it were for the whole of Srebrenica I would never hit you, therefore you needn't be afraid of me." And Mr. Ivanovic remembered this because there was in contrast to the others who were not like this particular guard, the others who beat himself and the other prisoners daily. He remembers, Your Honour, a particular incident involving Rado Pejic, whose beard was set on fire, and he remembers that distinctly because it is not something that one would forget. This only lends to the type of incidents that they were subjected to during that period of time. He talks about the fact that on one particular occasion, he was taken to the receptionist room in the prison located in the prison, and he remembers that there were up to seven men present. He remembers Zulfo Tursunovic being present. He remembers Ahmo Tihic, someone he knew before, was present. He remembers Ismet Odjic [phoen] was present. Also Mandzic, whom he later met again as he was being exchanged. What was most important about this meeting, in addition to the individuals he named, was the fact that there was someone present whom he later recalled from television and newspaper. He recalled being before these men, bloodied, literally lying on the ground because he could not stand, and as he described the fact that this was -- this beating had been a result of days of daily beatings by the prisoners, he recalls the fact that he was bloodied before these men, they simply stood there and looked at him, while two of the other men said that they knew him. There was one particular man in the room that day, Your Honour, that he described, and he went to lengths to say at the time he didn't know who this person was but he said when he returned to the cell, the guards asked him, did you see Adela [phoen] or Naser or the boss? At the time, he didn't know who they were referring to, but he testified, Your Honour, that the individual who was in the room, this young man, was the same person he later saw from television and newspapers, and he recognised that person as Naser Oric. Naser Oric, one of the men who was in that room, as he laid on the floor bloodied and beaten. And he was returned to the cell where the beating continued of himself and the other prisoners. It did not end. He was not released, nor were the others released. The beating did not cease. And as I stated before, he remembered being interrogated and the Prosecution's exhibits will bear that out, and during the time that he was interrogated, Your Honour, he recalls there was -- the person who was interrogating him was wearing an olive drab jacket and he was interrogated on more than one occasion. But during that interrogation, Your Honour, the soldier who escorted him to the interrogation struck him on the head with a knife in front of the very man that he was being interrogated by and he said the person who was interrogating him didn't hit him or beat him. It was the soldier. But the soldier in the presence of the man interrogated him, struck him on the head with a knife causing him to bleed. Mr. Ivanovic also talked about the fact that a number of the injuries that he received was -- were in fact permanent and that as a result, he is disabled to this very day. He also recalls other particular incidents where girls were brought in or pieces of fire -- pieces of paper were lit so that they could see the guards or the other individuals beaten him could see because at the time it was dark. So they were beaten at night as well, and the light was provided by these pieces of paper that were lit. He also talked about Cane, Stanko Hrstic [phoen] who was a disabled prisoner. He remembers him because he remembers the fact that he was beaten repeatedly by soldiers, by the guards, who, when Cane would go to the toilet would wander off because he wanted to go home and would get lost and the soldiers beat him as a result. Something which lapped on more than one occasion and they beat him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson, I hate to interrupt you, but it seemed to me it was conceded yesterday that the Defence does not contest that cruel treatment actually did take place, and that killings with the reservation that they made did take place, but particularly with regard to cruel treatment. So I would suggest to you that you skip any details that you have in mind to refer to prove by way of proving that this one or that one or the other person or that other person were actually beaten, either at the prison or in the police station, and concentrate on the 7(3) responsibility that the accused is being charged with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I will tailor my submission with that in mind, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you just restrict yourself to the Prosecution alleges in the indictment that persons, individuals, from number 1 to number 7 were beaten up in these two places, you can then move to say, we have evidence to show that they were beaten up by X, Y, Z, or by unknown persons and deal with the possible responsibility of Naser Oric, where the perpetrators are known and where the perpetrators are unknown.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will tailor my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what is important to us rather than trying to find out who was beaten and who was wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will tailor my submission with that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise feel free to expand and reduce however you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Please feel free to interrupt me if I'm not following Your Honour's instructions in that regard. Next I would like to refer to one of the prisoners that died in the prison, Kostan Popovic who is listed in our indictment as having been killed in the prison. As I said before, Mr. Ivanovic testified that they were all beaten. He remembers Mr. Kostadin Popovic, known as Kosta and Kodjo [phoen] as well, and the Prosecution submits that in addition to Prosecution's Exhibit which indicates that Mr. Popovic actually did die, Mr. Ivanovic testified that at the time that Mr. Popovic died, he was beaten just before, as they were beaten on a daily basis, not only Mr. Ivanovic but Mr. Ratko Nikolic as well, that people came, two men came to the prison where they placed Mr. Kostadin Popovic's body and it was wrapped up. Something was written down on a piece of paper. And he was taken away. Incidently, Mr. Popovic was also interrogated by Hamid Salihovic and we can show that via Prosecution's exhibit P46. Another individual that died in the prison was Milisav Milanovic, also known as Mico from Sase. Mr. Ivanovic also testified that Mr. Milanovic was beaten and he died as a result, with the very same procedure taking place where individuals came to the cell, he was wrapped, and a piece of paper was written down and placed in his pocket. You may recall, Your Honour, that Mr. Popovic's son testified, Nikola Popovic, testified and identified the body of his father, also stated that when his father's body was being examined by Dr. Stankovic, that there was a piece of paper with the name and information about Kostadin Popovic and the fact that he had been in prison in Srebrenica, confirming in fact what the other prisoners had said about this piece of paper. Next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'll discuss this with Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser as I discuss everything else, and we are going to try to make your life much easier, Ms. Richardson. We are exempting you from the need to indicate to us evidence that there is in this case tending to prove the death or the killing of all the persons mentioned in the indictment with the exception of Bogdanovic, whom you concede there is no evidence, and with the cruel treatment of all the persons mentioned in -- for the purpose of count 2, with the exception of Milevic [phoen] or whatever the name is that you conceded earlier on this morning there is no evidence about. Whatever. I mean, I'm sure she knows the name. I'm hopeless at names. All you need to concentrate about is whether the rest that is required under the law for the purpose of the rule 98 bis exercise only, as it relates to command responsibility, 7 -- under 7(3), and that's it. Make the submissions on those and skip all submissions tending to prove who was killed or who was beaten up. I think I'm making the position very clear. I mean those of course will be extremely valuable points that will need to be considered later on but for the time being, we are not going to enter into the question whether there is enough evidence to prove that a person who is known to be dead was actually killed, et cetera. I mean that's -- we -- I think we are making the position very clear. That doesn't come in the Rule 98 bis. We have ambivalent and sometimes dubious evidence, but that's something that until now is not important. Later on, it might become extremely important. Later on we might well come to the conclusion that you have got evidence with regard to a few but not to all. Or to none, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, then I'll be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes: We are interested in the following. Is there evidence that beatings and killings took place in both places?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do you submit or maintain that Naser Oric should be held criminally responsible under 7(3) for both the killings and the cruel treatment, both as -- both those committed in the police station and those committed in the prison? Submissions with regard to alleged knowledge and submissions with regard to alleged failure to prevent or to punish. That's what we are interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour. With that in mind, I would move to the next witness with respect to what Naser Oric knew about the prisoners and just briefly refer you back to the testimony of Mira Stojanovic, the wife of Slavoljub [phoen] Filipovic. There was testimony from Mr. Okanovic and Mr. Filipovic about the fact that they spoke to Naser Oric via radio about the fact that his wife and the children were being held prisoner in Srebrenica. There is a document, Your Honour, that I'll refer to in a moment with respect to that fact. But perhaps I should also point out to Your Honours the testimony of Pyers Tucker who stated that when he and General Morillon met with Naser Oric in Srebrenica, Naser Oric was directly asked whether or not he was holding prisoners and Naser Oric did not answer the question. In fact, he said, "Yes, taking prisoners is not practical and we don't do it." When General Morillon asked him whether he was holding prisoners a couple of times he never responded to the question. Lo and behold, though, a few days later, Colonel Tucker testified that Naser Oric drives up in a Mercedes, which I'm sure you will recall, and leads them to the area of the PTT building where he goes in and later on, immediately thereafter, a prisoner is brought out, and that Colonel Tucker said, and I quote, "The man looked like the Jews who were rescued in 1945 from the German concentration camps. His arms were like sticks, his stomach was completely shrunk. He was unable to stand, unable to speak." And although after that incident, Your Honour, clearly Naser Oric knew that there were prisoners there, the other prisoners remained and, again, you indicated there was not necessary to go into who was killed in the prison, but I would just point out that following that incident other prisoners remained behind and they succumbed to the beatings in the prison and they were -- they were killed thereafter. Let me submit to Your Honours with respect to -- that is with respect to knowledge, and of course, Naser Oric was also aware, as Mrs. Sellers pointed out, that there were prisoners that were held in the prison, in the months before 1992. He as aware of how they were treated. He observed them firsthand, and I should point out that the female witnesses testified in regards to whether or not Naser Oric had actual knowledge in 1993, the female witnesses testified that Zulfo Tursunovic visited the cell very often and he asked about why it was that the male prisoners looked beaten and bloodied. The male prisoners themselves testified to that effect. Zulfo Tursunovic, close associate of Naser Oric, a member of the OS staff, in fact based on the interview by Naser Oric he was placed in charge of the prison. And I will just refer you to tape 3. This is page 4 of 27. Naser Oric in response to the role of Zulfo Tursunovic, Naser Oric stated that the man had absolutely no high education at all but he had been in various prisons for 14 years and knew and had spent quite a lot of time with lawyers and had some kind of idea about how they worked. He also knew about things which -- how things were supposed to function in the prison, what prison is supposed to look like. He spent 13 and a half years. He knew how guards were supposed to behave towards prisoners and how prisoners were supposed to behave towards guards. I submit, Your Honour, Zulfo Tursunovic, in fact, on his very -- almost daily visits to the prison was very much aware of the state of the prisoners, Naser Oric very much was aware based on his own words that Zulfo Tursunovic had been visiting the prisons and he should have been informed or should have inquired at least as to the condition of the prisoners. And again with respect to Hamid Salihovic, the person who was the chief of security and intelligence, interrogating witnesses -- excuse me, prisoners, Naser Oric being fully aware that this interrogation was going on of the prisoners and he said as much with respect to the role of Hamid Salihovic, what was his job, whether it was his job to inform Naser Oric of the status of the Serb soldiers, if he maintained information. Naser Oric responded, "Well of course," as he was one of the officers or one of the people who had some kind of military knowledge and a man who had been the head of the police in Srebrenica before the war and he's a man who knew the system of investigation. It's logical he would have asked the questions in the way he thought they should have been asked, clearly aware, Your Honour, that Hamid Salihovic had been interrogating prisoners knowing fully well that prisoners were kept in Srebrenica. And I should go next of course to what Naser Oric observed himself and I already talked about the fact that he saw the condition of Mr. Ivanovic, he saw the condition of Pejic as he was removed and I would submit to you that this was not just inquiry notice, this was actual knowledge and notice of the condition of the prisoners at the time. With respect to whether or not he was the commander of the military police, Your Honour, I submit that you look again, review the military log, the memo pad, the memo pad this states that the military police belongs to the -- excuse me, the military police belongs to the military, not to the War Presidency. When Naser Oric was asked whether or not what his relationship was to the military police in the interview, when he was asked, "Is the military police a branch of the military under which -- of which you were the commander," he said "Yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you again, Ms. Richardson, but this applies to you, to Mr. Di Fazio, to Mr. Doria later on, there is evidence tending to show what you're saying, there is evidence tending to show differently. That being the case, we are definitely not going into the question of what was the proper placement of the military police at the time, not for the purpose of the Rule 98 bis. So take it that you don't need to go into any details or any argumentation or submissions to prove to us what was the proper standing of the military police within the structure, if at all, existing at the time. Keep in mind that there is evidence for and there is evidence against. And that we will decide later on obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Let me sum up by saying this: The evidence shows that there was a connection, that there was a superior subordinate relationship, that Naser Oric did in fact have with the -- not only the military police who were directly involved with the prisoners, guarding them, as well as from the very moment they arrived in Srebrenica, at the police station, as well as at the prison. This relationship as well extends to Hamid Salihovic who interrogated the prisoners and it extends to Zulfo Tursunovic, and with respect to, again, knowledge, Naser Oric had actual knowledge. There is a case to answer with respect to 1 and 2. He visited the prisons as well as his subordinates were involved. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think now it's Mr. Di Fazio's turn. Would you come in front, Mr. Di Fazio, or do you prefer to stay where you are? MR. DI FAZIO: I'm happy to stay here. I just need the lectern, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The Trial Chamber would have course be very much interested in hearing what you have to say with regard to the other two crimes, wanton destruction and plunder and the elements. With regard to the evidence, again, please do not waste your and our time to tell us which villages were attacked and when, and which villages had houses destroyed, et cetera. Concentrate on whether the houses destroyed in any particular village satisfy the -- one of the elements required, in other words whether we are talking of significant or insignificant wanton destruction. I know that the question of necessity is going to be dealt with by Mr. Doria and when you come to plunder, again, I mean we don't need submissions to tell us that there were people taking food, livestock. Perhaps you can concentrate on the importance or non-importance of the killing of the pigs and the taking away of things that are not necessary for one's livelihood, like food and clothing, given the circumstances. And concentrate on other matters. Also you need to address the question of civilians that were supposedly taking part in this alleged plundering, and how the accused may or may not fit in when the evidence shows that it was civilians and not military fighters or soldiers - call them whatever you like, so that I do not get into the merit of that - who were under his control directly or indirectly. Did I get through to you? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, you certainly did, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... five minutes, so perhaps you can introduce the subject and then continue afterwards. If I have created problems for you please come forward and tell me. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't think so, but I'll -- perhaps if I just do my introductory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I think you ought to do. MR. DI FAZIO: The issues that you've raised and extract them from the submissions I had prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, just by way of law first, I certainly don't intend to belabour these points. There is not much in the way of controversy as far as the plunder and destruction is concerned. But the requirements under Article 3(B), of course, require destruction. The Prosecution submission is that it is sufficient - and in this case of course we are dealing with villages and hamlets - it's sufficient if we can demonstrate to you that there is evidence of part of a village having been destroyed. That is the Prosecution's submission and that's the way I'm going to proceed to evaluate the evidence in order to establish a case to answer. Furthermore in this particular indictment, there is no reference to devastation in the indictment at all so that any differences that might exist between wanton destruction and devastation, if they exist, are not matters that are going to have to trouble you. The indictment doesn't use that expression that is contained in the Statute. So devastation is not something you have to worry about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's how we were looking at it in any event. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. The -- another element that needs to be proved of course, is that the destruction is wanton. If Your Honours please, the wantonness is a matter that is determined not just by the scale and extent of damage but the manner in which it is damaged -- in which the damage is inflicted. And the Prosecution's submission is that that element should not trouble you, as the evidence in this case demonstrates that the torching of the structures, the buildings and so on could only have been deliberate and intentional and done with a view to inflicting damage in the absence of good reason, military necessity. And again, I say that issues of recklessness and negligence are not going to trouble you in this case as well. Then of course we come to the third element that's required for destruction, and that's the issue of military necessity. On the Prosecution case, the overwhelming bulk of the evidence in this case shows that houses buildings and the structures that are so dear and essential to farming communities up in the mountains of Bosnia where these events took place were looted and put to the torch. They -- the evidence does not show that machine-gun nests were being destroyed, that ammunition dumps were being destroyed, that trenches where village guards found themselves at night or during the day were being targeted and destroyed. It overwhelmingly shows that structures that were used by the local peasants in the area were being destroyed. And the Prosecution submission is essentially that that evidence, that overwhelming evidence, clearly demonstrates no conceivable military necessity for the destruction of those individual houses, barns, farm houses, shops, gyms, et cetera. But furthermore, the fury with which these attacks were launched against these hill side villages and villages in the area is also evidence that you can take into account in considering the question of whether or not the Prosecution has demonstrated a lack or an absence of military necessity. What the evidence does show in the Prosecution submission, and it points only in one way, only one way, is that the principal object of these attacks was the plunder and destruction of these particular houses. If Your Honours please, that's briefly -- I need to finish a couple of matters on military necessity but that very briefly is my introductory comment insofar as destruction is concerned. I'll deal with plunder later. I take it -- I had prepared to take you through the evidence, not chapter and verse, but to go through each attack and highlight the extent of damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to do that. We have done that already and we do not have problems there. Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:. Thank you. What I'll do then is during the break I'll reevaluate my evidence, cut out what's unnecessary, and that will help us all get through today faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a break, shall we say 25 minutes or 30 minutes. It depends, whichever you prefer, Mr. Di Fazio, 25 or 30 minutes? MR. DI FAZIO: That's fine, if Your Honours please. Perhaps the -- I think I can deal with it in 25 minutes if you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours. On the issue of military submission, yesterday Mr. Jones referred you to the List Hostages Trial case conducted before the United States --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Military submission or military if necessity? MR. Di FAZIO: The name of the case is The List Hostages Trial case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, all right, no, no, because you said "military submission." Oh, I see. I see what you mean. Okay. All right. I got that. MR. DI FAZIO: And he quoted from that -- from that case. But he preceded it, and I'll take you back to that in just a moment, but he preceded that with the submission that the Prosecution's approach in this case is to ask you to, and I quote, "assume, to guess, that any damage to property was unlawful." In other words, that it was conducted in the absence of military necessity. And then he took to you that case which commented on what might or might not constitute military necessity. I don't need to quote his direct words because it's made up in various parts, but one of the matters that was said to be a relevant inquiry for military necessity is whether the actions compel the complete submission of the enemy. The destruction of these small hamlets and villages, the destruction of their homes, the killing of their pigs and burning down of the barns and haystacks and so on, in the Prosecution's submission, can in no rational way be viewed as being directed in any way to bringing about the complete submission of the VRS or the JNA, and at the same time, as I said to you earlier, it points unerringly to another motive behind these attacks. So that's one aspect of the matters that he raised. The other relevant matter that was referred to in that case was military necessity might be demonstrated or shown or exist where you can see that it's facilitating the safety of his forces or facilitating the success of his operations. And the Prosecution submission is, on that matter, that in this evidential scenario, there is a complete absence of any evidence of the villages, the inhabitants of these villages, the farmers and their wives and so on, posing any threat to the safety of the attackers. All of the evidence overwhelmingly shows that they were going about their normal business on the day of the attack. They were woken out of their beds or they were preparing for lunch. So it's inconceivable to see how burning a haystack or a barn or a house could in any way facilitate the safety of his forces or the success of his operations. In this regard, you may want to consider the role that the village guard system had to play insofar as it relates to military necessity. The evidence here was uniformly consistent through -- from all of the Prosecution witnesses. The clear theme that came out in all of their evidence is that these village guards were local creations, village creations, community creations, obviously made up as the worsening -- as tensions worsened in the former Bosnia, and the overwhelming purpose -- well, not overwhelming, the only purpose of these village guards was protection of the local village and no other purpose. All of the Prosecution witnesses told you that. That's their evidence. It may have been challenged by the Defence, but as you know we are not here to discuss the weight or the truth of that claim, but that's their evidence. It was there to protect their villages. And again, the overwhelming, clear evidence of all of the witnesses was that these village guards were not sophisticated operations, no military paraphernalia apart from their -- their light weapons. And again the village guards operated in the main only at night, might go up and sit in their trenches up above the village and look out over the village and guard the place, but they operated mainly at night. During the day these farmers were doing their normal business, carrying out their farming business. So -- and furthermore, on the evidence that's been presented by the Prosecution witnesses who described to you how the attacks unfolded, how the attacks unfolded, it's pretty clear that the target was not and never was anything to do with this village guard system. They didn't attack anyone in the trenches first. They didn't try and isolate men who were part of the village guard. They were just indiscriminate. So it's -- in the Prosecution's submission, the village guard system cannot play -- play no part in establishing the presence of military necessity for the destruction of haystacks, barns, and so on. So that's what I want to say to you on that particular issue. The other elements, of course, that you need to have for -- to establish these charges is the wilfulness of the destruction and the nexus between the destruction and the armed conflict. I don't propose to address you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to. MR. DI FAZIO: It's pretty obvious from the circumstances of this case, that's not going to trouble you in this case. So I turn to plunder, 3(E) and again I don't need to address you at length here. Issues of the unlawful appropriation of property in armed conflict are fine questions that aren't going to trouble you in this case. When the plunder took place in this case, it's clear it was gone, and it was gone for good. And there is no question that you can infer, in fact it's the only inference available to you on the evidence, that there was an intention to acquire possession as against the villagers who owned the property. And it was clearly of sufficient value to them. Now, the issue that you wanted me to address you specifically on that arises in this context, that's the issue of food. And I'll deal with you there. I'll deal with that issue now. Excuse me. Before I get into it I would just like to make one or two comments about the manner in which the Prosecution -- the Defence dealt with this issue. Mr. Jones posed the rhetorical question to you: "How can it be criminal for the poor, desperate, starving civilians to steal food to feed themselves and their children? Because that's the evidence of the Prosecution. I know I would do it. I believe Your Honours would do it. I think any decent human being would steal food to feed their starving children, wives, and themselves. The Prosecution may require people to starve or to be judged criminals but Your Honours should not do so." The concerns of Mr. Jones might have been laid to rest if he'd read the indictment just a little more carefully, in particular in paragraph 35. If -- do Your Honours have the indictment? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I was anticipating what you were going to say, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: The -- the -- well, you can see what the scheme of the indictment is. It -- paragraphs 29 through to 36 deal with the crime base but the issue of plunder is -- is dealt with in the main in -- it's dealt with in paragraph 35. It says, in the course of these attacks in eastern Bosnia between the dates, units under the command and control of Naser Oric plundered Bosnian Serb property. Namely, and I stress that word, namely, cattle, furniture, television sets. You contrast that with the wording that is used in respect of destruction. In addition, Bosnian Serb property, including buildings and dwellings, were unlawfully destroyed. In the case of plunder, it's restrictive, in the case of destruction, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Provided that is clear, we are happy with that. MR. DI FAZIO: That lays to rest the issue, and it reveals that this case is not about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not about the taking of military hardware, weapons, tanks, rifles, or whatever was mentioned during the testimony, and you are also excluding food and clothing. All right. MR. DI FAZIO: There is an exhaustive list, cattle, furniture, television sets, just three items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because much of the evidence that we received here was evidence as to the alleged plunder, looting, of food, clothing, military hardware. MR. DI FAZIO: That's all relevant evidence because it shows widespread plunder, but the enumerated items are there, and that's what you have to be happy about before you can find -- in order to find a case to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, cattle is food, that's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but we come to cattle now. That's my next question obviously. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, cattle can be transformed into food. You can kill it and you can eat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you don't do it on the spot. MR. DI FAZIO: You don't do it on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's only McDonald's that do that. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's deal with cattle. I mean we've heard that cattle was taken away and the submission by the Defence is that, given the circumstances, this was precisely essential for survival. MR. DI FAZIO: There are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is your submission that cattle was not -- does not fall within that category and that essentially it was wanton appropriation? MR. DI FAZIO: Essentially that is our submission because otherwise it couldn't have been included in the indictment. It has to be on the Prosecution's case otherwise you have to remove that in your findings. In any event, it's also an issue that arises in the context of necessity, general defence of necessity that was raised by Mr. Jones yesterday. My colleague Mr. Doria is going to deal with the overall issue of necessity. So perhaps it's best if he deals with that particular topic. But in any event, in so far as the general crime base is concerned, for plunder, that's what I'm going to deal with and I will us straight to you when -- examples of when cattle were taken. So, there we have the submissions on what precisely you must look at in order to find a case to answer the sorts of properties. Can I just return briefly to the issue of large-scale destruction? Mr. Jones yesterday submitted that large-scale destruction is necessary and he complained that no inventory had been provided by the Prosecution of damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can skip that, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: My submission is very simple. You don't have to. If you want an inventory you get it out of the words of the witnesses who came here and told you of the extent of the damage. If Your Honours please, throughout the evidence on my analysis of the evidence of the witnesses, in each case, in each little place, Fakovici and Radijevici, et cetera, in each little village and the surrounding hamlets that you have mentioned in the indictment, the witnesses spoke of what is plainly large scale destruction and at times utter and total destruction. Witness after witness came back -- came here and told you of going back to their -- their hamlets and finding nothing but the foundations and weeds growing there where once it had been a thriving community. Witness after witness spoke to you of seeing entire villages ablaze and witness after witness spoke to you of seeing not only entire villages ablaze but whole areas with villages ablaze. You remember the evidence of one particular witness, just give me a moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I don't think you need elaborate on the extent of the destruction that is alleged, and about what -- about which we heard enough, I think, during the case for the Prosecution. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would rather concentrate on plunder again and my questions to you is, I think, have you finalised concluded your submissions on the taking away of cattle? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So my next question to you excluding the taking away of cattle at least for argument's sake, you're left with appropriation of some household appliances like televisions, et cetera. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it your submission that there is enough in the evidence which would justify the jurisdiction of this Tribunal to deal with such a count? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Yes. These were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is the extent according to you. MR. DI FAZIO: Does it rise to a sufficient level of seriousness? Is that Your Honour's inquiries? Yes, the evidence of many of the witnesses revealed large-scale plunder. It revealed houses being stripped of their possessions. The witness who spoke about Bradjevina described his house, I think it was Stanisa Stevanovic described his house being emptied. His video recorder, his fridge, his -- and households goods being taken out of the homes. These were simple peasant farmers, if Your Honours please. To take away these possessions -- and not rich people. To take away these possessions has an impact upon these people that is fundamental in the Prosecution's submission, and to take away their cattle, you take away their cattle, you take away one of the basic building blocks of their community. If you destroy their pigs, you take away one of the basic building blocks of their community. So it's not just a question of the odd television set or the odd freezer being taken away by an over-enthusiastic pillager. The general thrust of the evidence is that the houses were being emptied, pillaged. The scenario that Mira Stojanovic described when she drove back through Bjelovac in the yellow Mercedes Benz, I don't know if you recall that evidence, as she was taken back to Srebrenica to start her capture was of hordes of people all over t place, all over the town, systematically stripping it. So you can't say that the plunder was insignificant or consisted of the isolated television set or cow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes but Mr. Di Fazio taking you back -- taking you to task again because after all you yourself highlighted, emphasised, the use of the name -- of the word "namely" in paragraph 35 of the indictment. Just as that "namely" then restricts the category of objects allegedly plundered such as cattle, you then say furniture and television sets. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much evidence do you submit there is showing that furniture was taken away, and how much evidence is there according to you as to the appropriation of television sets? There is definitely one testimony regarding practical pillaging of one house. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. One house. What about the rest? And my question to you when you count everything, add up everything and put everything in one basket recognition what are you talking about? Would it justify the jurisdiction of -- or the intervention of the jurisdiction of this Tribunal? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, particularly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget cattle, because cattle s another -- I mean, if you then put it together with cattle, if you're right in your submission on cattle, then obviously the whole scenario changes, but if you're not right in your submission on cattle, then what's your position with regard to the remaining things? MR. DI FAZIO: I understand. Your Honours, the Prosecution in that case must rely on general descriptions of plunder. A number of witnesses spoke of household possessions being taken. Now, the Prosecution would submit to you that that's enough to -- that that must imply furniture, as enumerated in the -- as set out in the indictment. And that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You chose the word furniture, not -- the Prosecutor chose the word furniture, not we. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Furniture means furniture. MR. DI FAZIO: It does. It does, but household possessions encompasses furniture. On any reasonable reading of the use of that expression, household possessions, it must encompass furniture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But for example a television set is obviously not being considered as furniture. Likewise I put it to you that a tape recorder or a video recorder is also not furniture. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So any evidence that there is relating to a tape recorder or a video recorder or a kettle for that matter, it's not furniture so why should we consider it? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, yes, I agree that video recorder is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want to make your life difficult but I'm just presenting you with some problems. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand. If Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry for the interruption, and I will try to interrupt you as little as I can, Mr. Di Fazio, but these are obviously problems that we are facing and that this is why we wanted to hear your submissions. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. If Your Honours please, the wording in the indictment could have been different but there it is. And the fall back position that the Prosecution must have, the only submission that it can present to you on -- in this respect is that where witnesses spoke of general plunder and the taking of household possessions, that must of necessity have included furniture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's an inference that you're asking us to make. MR. DI FAZIO: It's an available inference to you. It's available to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's your submission. All right. Go ahead. MR. DI FAZIO: Households possessions must of necessity include furniture. And the witnesses of course who we called weren't in a position 12 years later and in the circumstances in which they found themselves during the attack to be able to enumerate item by item what was being taken from their houses. So that's the difficulty the Prosecution faced, but it's overcome by the fact that they did refer to household possessions. So if Your Honours please, can I just return now to the issue of widespread destruction or is it the case that you don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I don't think we need to hear about widespread destruction. We have gone village by village, and took account of the percentage of houses and sometimes the number of houses that were indicated by various witnesses as having been torched, destroyed or whatever. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- MR. DI FAZIO: If I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we've -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I can -- just one further matter that I might raise then in respect of plunder, and that's this. In going through the evidence again, I looked at the evidence relating to plunder in Radijevici, which is one of the small hamlets close to Fakovici, and I couldn't find any significant evidence of any plunder there at all. Certainly damage, destruction, but not plunder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is one of the notes we have made too. MR. DI FAZIO: So I don't think you need to have to trouble yourselves with looking at evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Radijevici. We have it in -- MR. DI FAZIO: So that really just leaves me, then, I suppose, if Your Honours please, with the issue of the soldiers and the civilians and who was conducting what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't mention it because I wasn't quite clear whether it was going to be dealt by you or by Mr. Doria because 7(3) responsibility seems to be under 4, which is under Doria. However, that's your problem. I mean, if you want to make submissions now, make submissions now. MR. DI FAZIO: Perhaps we will share it to a certain extent. I'll make the submissions that I want to, and then Mr. Doria can pick up anything that, hopefully, that I leave out. I'm really just focusing on the actual crime base itself, what happened on the ground in these villages. There is a lot of evidence in this case that indicates that the fighters who attacked these villages themselves plundered and destroyed. It's -- you can -- I can take you through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I don't think you need to because we have got it itemised, village by village. MR. DI FAZIO: Can I just take you to two or three points. I won't trouble you for long on this because I want to highlight that. The Defence would have you look at these attacks as some sort of maelstrom of civilians and attackers falling, coming down over a hill and the impossibility of identifying who is who. Well, the witnesses that the Prosecution brought here didn't have -- didn't experience that difficulty. Milenko Stevanovic is -- he came here and spoke to you about Ratkovici and he said, page 1618, that he saw a combination of soldiers and civilians, both of them. Not just civilians but what he called soldiers, taking away cattle and other goods, cattle from the sheds. So he was able to distinguish, and that is his evidence, and that is enough for a prima facie case. If later you decide, oh, well, look he couldn't have possibly said that to me, that's another matter. But as things stand that's his evidence. So you've got soldiers taking away or fighters taking away property from -- from him, from his village. Stanisa Stevanovic also spoke about Bradjevina, and again he said that he could see soldiers and civilians burning stables and taking away the cattle. Sorry, would you just give me a moment? Oh, yes. Mr. Stevanovic painted a picture of cooperation between soldiers and civilians. He was asked, page 1494, "Who took away these items? Who actually physically carried away the lighter items and the food?" And he said, "The soldiers who entered the houses were taking things out. But of course they had civilians who also helped them pick things out and carry these items off." There you have it, that's prima facie evidence of soldiers, fighters, intimately involved in the process. Just two or three more on this because they provide good examples of the sort of evidence that you can look at to conclude that there was the fighters who were involved in the destruction and the plunder. Slavoljub Zikic also provided you with evidence of the soldiers' taking away his cow and his calf and also taking away items. Mira Stojanovic, you remember she was the lady who was captured in Bjelovac with her children and taken off to Srebrenica. As I said, she saw armed soldiers all carrying backpacks and rucksacks on the road back to Srebrenica as she was driving along in a car. But she saw both soldiers and civilians, that's her evidence, walking around Bjelovac carrying bags of looted goods. And Ratko Nikolic, who also spoke of events in Kravica, I want to quote from his evidence together -- specifically. He said he saw armed men assisting civilians take things from the houses -- from their homes. Question: "Did you see any items being removed from houses?" "Yes." "Who did that?" Answer: "It was done by people who went to the villages to collect things and they were escorted by soldiers with weapons. I was hiding in a hollow tree and could see them taking my things away." That's the fellow who got shot in the foot and didn't make good his escape with his wife. He was captured. And then he continued. Question: "In Opravdici did you see anyone taking possessions away from the houses?" Answer: "Yes." Question: "At that time, the people who were taking possessions, were they in company with armed men?" Answer: "Yes." So there is clear evidence in this case of just soldiers alone or fighters taking plunder, taking goods, and there is other evidence, a lot of other evidence in the case, that armed soldiers actually destroyed. That is just about completes my submissions. I've got a few more matters I want to raise so I won't be long. I just want to take you very briefly, remind you of the evidence of Mira Stojanovic on the issue of destruction, because she is a good witness to provide you with a snapshot into the events in the -- during one of these attacks, Bjelovac, because of course you remember she was captured and she was kept by the soldiers who were actually fighting from her house and from another house that she was taken to. And you recall her evidence regarding destruction, page 3384. She was leaving her house during -- in order to be taken to the second place in Bjelovac where the fighting continued until nightfall. And she was able to see this. In respect of the place that she had lived in. As she was leaving, "What was said or done?" Answer: "One of the soldiers said set the house on fire immediately. We left and I didn't look back, because I didn't dare to. But I suppose that's what they did. They set the house on fire." Question: "Okay. You didn't look back. Tell the Trial Chamber why you suppose that? Why do you suppose that? Did you hear anything or see anything that makes you think or say -- think that or say that?" Answer: "I suppose that because one of the soldiers said to the others, burn the house immediately. It sounded like an order." And she told you that as she drove through Bjelovac the next day in the yellow Mercedes on her way to her confinement in Srebrenica, that her house had been destroyed. So there you have it, direct, clear-as-a-bell evidence of an order by soldiers for destruction during an actual attack. And what was the possible reason for that destruction? There was none. That is also evidence of not only soldiers directly participating in destruction of dwellings but an utter lack of any conceivable military necessity. This was wantonness at its worst. So if Your Honours please, that just about wraps up my submissions. The -- you find limited evidence of the destruction and the plunder in the documentary evidence. I'm not going to take you to it in any great detail. But P84, the memo pad, provides you with a little snapshot into discussions on this topic conducted in Mr. Oric's inner circle.
