Page 49 of P84, they were discussing some -- it's minutes of the meeting on the 10th of January 1993, discussing an operation, military operation, and it's -- from reading it, it appears to be excerpts of what each man commented on at this meeting, and Zulfo apparently is quite -- is requesting that priority be given to the operation towards Jezero or Jezero. Unfortunately it's not clear, but the note here says, "it burned down 42 villages." Then Ibro wants to participate in all operations. Nedzad goes on too say that he participated in all operations. Safet expresses his view that an attack on Bratunac would be better and Ahmo says that he wants to go for Jezero, and Mr. Oric then says "the next operation will be Jezero. Let us reach an agreement." Ahmo then goes on it to talk of the whole operation being planned and says "We will mop up the whole area, but the left wing is stronger than the right one where they have more men." Skelani was burned down, and then Ahmo says, "Arson should not be allowed before people from Skelani take back their belongings". So it's not just the civilians who told you about the destruction, the plunder. If Your Honours please, this case is not about the pursuing or the hounding of a commander of soldiers and his fighters who was struggling to secure food for themselves and their starving families. I'd like to pose some rhetorical questions. If that were so, if that were the reason, the fundamental reason behind these attacks, why was it necessary to burn down people's houses or barns or their haystacks? Why was it necessary to burn a gym? Why was it necessary to burn down a village shop? Why was it necessary to fire bullet holes into grave stones? Why was all that necessary? It's about food and survival, as the Defence would have you believe. Why was it necessary to slaughter pigs, kill them, if it's about food and survival. Why was it necessary to take their cattle and their household possessions? Why was it necessary to kill old men and women? Why was it necessary to slice off the genitalia of a --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour, there is not part of the indictment, this is purely inflammatory on my learned friend's part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not easily inflamed, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There is a public following. MR. DI FAZIO: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't mean to inflame. I mean to address you on the issue of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones is right. You're saying rhetorical questions. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I don't find at all rhetorical -- the question is if you're trying to secure food for your family, your starving population, why should you take cattle away? Of course you would take cattle away. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, but what about those other matters that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then stick take to the other matters. MR. DI FAZIO: And they -- and they -- they demonstrate, if Your Honours please, that there was a wilful intention to plunder and to destroy on the part of these attackers. That was the purpose with which I referred you to those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Where would you fit the slaughtering of the pigs, Mr. Di Fazio? Under which count? MR. DI FAZIO: It's clearly the destruction of Serb property. Not only that, of course, the significance of the slaughter of that particular beast, type of beast, is -- the significance of it is clear. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, those are the submissions I want to make to you on the crime base. The crime base provides you with a solid platform for the plunder and the destruction. And I hope that the Prosecution has allayed any fears that is this is a case about the prosecution of a commander of -- that it's a case about the -- hounding a man who was trying to survive. The Prosecution is well aware and has never challenged any of the hardships that people suffered in Srebrenica. The Prosecution is not focusing on that. It's focusing on those attacks and with respect the crime base has provided you with a platform with which to look at all of the other issues involved of command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Doria? I see here under point 4 that you will be dealing with the general defence of necessity which of course is important to deal with. Again, wanton destruction and plunder, please do not repeat any -- anything that has been stated by Mr. Di Fazio. And then elements I would say as -- are criminal responsibility, I would imagine, and you are dealing only with 7(3) command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So don't try to take it away from Mr. Wubben who will deal with 7(1) responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you, Your Honours. I would first start by discussing the issue of necessity. The concept of necessity that was brought yesterday. This is because when Your Honour asked Mr. Jones if he was considering making a submission to the effect that furniture could have been also used for food or whatever, he made such submission to the effect that furniture could be exchanged for food also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't mention furniture to start with. And secondly, Mr. Jones did not make a submission, as you put it. Mr. Jones referred to the testimony of someone. I forgot who. I think it would be Dr. Mujkanovic or whoever it was, when the question was put to him, and that that witness according to Mr. Jones, had stated of course they would take these other things. They would exchange them for food later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Yes. What is our position is that as Mr. Di Fazio has correctly stated, that we are not considering plunder, his plunder of food as such but plunder of property which can be used by whatever purpose, which does not interest us at this stage. We are interested in the crime of plunder as such, which is prohibited under international law. And then, as Mr. Di Fazio has focused on specific evidence which shows that plunder was indeed acts which amount to plunder were indeed committed and the specific items which we have charged in the indictment, like cattle, furniture and other items which evidence shows clearly that were taken away unlawfully. As for the concept of necessity, first of all I would like to say that the concept of necessity is -- has been until recently when it was introduced in Article 31 of the ICC Statute much of a concept of comparative law. It has been introduced in national jurisdictions but in an international setting, it has been very often confronted with the concept of duress. And commentators who have reviewed it carefully, and I will address Your Honours and my learned colleagues, friends from the Defence, through a book by Professor Cassese co-authored together by Mr. John Jones, where Professor Kajan Bozve [phoen] very carefully addresses, advises who's linked with necessity. Well, under there essentially three elements in the concept of necessity. The first element that there should be an imminent threat standing or continuing. The second element there should be necessary and reasonable measures, and the third element, that the intention should be to avoid a greater harm. This is the concept of conflict of interests where the person who commits the crime is pretending to commit a lesser evil. Even if we admit that just for a moment this is not our submission but if you admit just for a moment that the crime of plunder was committed out of a necessity because people were starving, the problem is that if you take food or you take furniture, those items which we charged, from civilians, then you put those civilians in the same situation, and then we will have a situation where the conflict of interests is changing life for life, which is prohibited actually when we talk about necessity. Necessity is about avoiding a greater harm in relation to the one that you are pretending to -- that you commit. Next, I would like to say that the concept of necessity, as my colleague Di Fazio has already said, that it also fails when you see that the plundering of property was accompanied by acts of destruction, acts of killing, acts of maltreat and so on and so on, so there is no justification for plundering because they -- the civilians were starving or because the military were starving. There was no justification for adding, destroying, wantonly destroying property, and killing and committing other barbaric acts against civilians. This is what I basically want to say about necessity. Moving further into the question of command responsibility, again I would like to emphasise that our case is not about plunder of food. It's about plunder of property, which is a crime under international law. No matter what is the purpose of the acts that were committed. Concerning command responsibility, we already stated in our pre-trial brief that there were three elements that we need to prove for command responsibility, to attach. First of all that there was a superior subordinate relationship, second that the accused knew or had reasons to know that the crimes were committed, and the third that he failed to prevent or punish those acts. Concerning the concept of superior and subordinate relationship, the Defence yesterday arose issues of whether the armoured units, armed forces under Naser Oric were at all organised forces within the meaning of international humanitarian law, and the Defence raises issues like absence of uniforms, barracks, and ranks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Doria, I have to stop you here. That is a matter that we are going to decide later on. Not now at this stage of the Rule 98 bis because there is evidence, different kinds of evidence, tending to prove different kinds of things. So skip that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: The Defence also raised the issue of VMS [phoen] also. If Your Honours would like me to attach on that issue also on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Attach on whatever the situation was, whether they were organised or not organised, what is there in the evidence that would suffice for the trier of facts, trier of facts, to reach a verdict of guilty later on? I mean it's -- if believed, obviously, I mean. It is what we -- what you need to submit. What do we have at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To establish the superior-subordinate relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: That's why I wanted first of all to address these issues, that we have evidence proving there was a command structure. There was a chain of command, there was ability to control the forces, there was ability to impose discipline. We have evidence showing that the units under Naser Oric conducted sustained military operations in certain instances were successful, like in the incidents in which we focus in our indictment. And we have evidence suggesting that, as the Defence conceded, and Mr. Naser Oric in his interview to the OTP also conceded, that fighters were not actually the ones plundering, for example, but civilians. Which means that the Defence and Mr. Naser Oric concede that the fighters were interested in respecting the rules of war, and this is also one of the conditions when we talk about organised armed forces, that there should be a command and control, that they have the ability to conduct sustained military operations, and they have the interest or the obligation that they abide by the rules of international humanitarian law. As for the argument --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Doria. You mentioned three things, command structure, okay, skip that. Then you said "ability to control the forces." What are you relying upon by way of evidence in asserting or in making that submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: When I talk about ability to control force I'm talking about the requirement of effective control, and Your Honour, I would address you to the recent Blaskic decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go to the evidence and direct us, address us to that part of the evidence which, according to you, would indicate on a prima facie basis of course, that the -- not only there wasn't only a command structure but that there was ability to control the forces, and then the next question that I will put to you is, again, where do we have to go in the evidence to agree with you that there was also the ability to impose discipline?

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: If Your Honour -- yes, I will address all these questions, of course. Let me just finish the -- if Your Honour will permit me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Yes, the issue of levee on mass which was raised and is very important to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: As I said the Defence raised the issue of levee on mass and first of all we don't agree with such a proposition, and second we submit that the Prosecution submitted even if there was a question of levee en masse, levee en masse under international law cannot be extended for long periods. If Your Honours may -- address you to the ICRC commentary on paragraph -- on Article 4(6) of the Third Geneva Conventions, it reads specifically that it should however be emphasised that mass levy can only be considered to exist during a very short period, during the actual invasion period. If resistance continues, the authority commanding the inhabitants who have taken up arms or the authority to which they profess allegiance must either replace them by sending regular units or must incorporate them in its regular forces, otherwise mass levy could not survive the total occupation of the territory which has been tried -- which it has tried in vain to defend. The Prosecution submits that indeed, if there was levee en masse, levee en masse ended when the 20th of May 19 -- 19 -- 1992, the Srebrenica armed forces were established. This you can find from -- this you can find from P73, formation of TO staff, P76, order confirming Naser Oric's command of Srebrenica TO staff of 27 June 1992. So the armed force, the civilian armed forces were established on the 20th of May 1992 and thereafter, and Naser Oric was confirmed by the army of Bosnia as commander of these forces and therefore the Srebrenica armed forces were integrated into the system, the chain of command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The chain of command went from the president of the Presidency of the -- of -- of -- of -- of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina through the 2nd Corps in Tuzla and down to the Srebrenica territorial forces. Now I would address you, Your Honours, to P -- to Exhibit number P114, a decision on organisation armed forces of the republic. P2, staff -- Main Staff of the Armed Forces District Defence Staff, Exhibit P279, formation of corps in zones under responsibility of the corps's command, and whatever is mentioned Exhibit P73 and P76, confirming Naser Oric as the commander of the armoured force of Srebrenica. Your Honour has requested me to indicate very briefly what are the indicatives of the -- the indicators of effective control that Naser Oric exercised over the units who commit -- which committed the crimes. As I would like to -- as I wanted to refer to the Blaskic decision, the appeal -- the recent Blaskic appeals decision, it has been stated that the indicators of effective control are a matter of facts, evidence of the case, rather than substantive law. The Prosecution submits that these indicators may include, also they are not restricted to them, to showing that the commander was the one who planned the actions, that the commander directly took part in the attacks, that the commander was in communication with the units, that the commander participated in meetings in which the results of the attacks were discussed. The Prosecution submits that if the evidence shows that this has happened, then we can make a conclusion that the commander was in effective control of the units which participated in the relevant -- in the relevant incidents. If Your Honour would like to -- I don't know if Your Honour want the -- this evidence in particular in relation to each of the incidents or generally. I could provide -- I have prepared either by incidents or just generally, if you want, I could just provide some examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In this part, I would rather keep my mouth shut and invite you to give indications.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Yes, what senior trial attorney Jan Wubben wanted to explain is that the example of the other colleagues that have already submitted their portions of our -- this submission, I also have prepared a binder containing the exhibits that could facilitate your understanding. But I will be any way citing the numbers of the exhibits and this also can facilitate because it will be on the record and can facilitate following what I was saying. In relation to -- I would go incidents by incident and I would like first of all to pick up the first incidents, the attacks which occurred in Ratkovici and Jezestica. Ratkovici was attacked on the 21st and the 27 of June, and Jezestica was attacked on the 8th of August 1992. Your Honours, we have evidence, you have given evidence to the effect that the units that participate in the attack in those two villages were units under the command of Naser Oric. For the attack of Ratkovici, the following were the units which participated. Srebrenica TO, 3 Maj Kragljivoda, Skenderovic TO. And Biljeg TO. Evidence confirming participation of these units, you can find, Your Honour, on Exhibit P87 which was confirmed by witness Sead Delic, Exhibit P95, Exhibit P95, Exhibit P94. In relation to the incident, the attack on Jezestica, the units which participated were Potocari TO, Sutjeska TO, Biljeg TO, Company Stari Grad. Again, you can find evidence of this in Exhibit P94 and Exhibit P95. Your Honour, our submission -- I would like to emphasise here that our submission is based in most of the case on circumstantial evidence. In the Celebici, the Appeals Chamber said that a case based on circumstantial evidence is one consisting of evidence of a number of different circumstances which taken in combination point to the guilt of the accused person because they would -- --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down because the interpreters do not have the text, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Doria, please slow down for the future because the interpreters very rightly so couldn't catch up with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Okay, thank. I will try --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but that was because he was reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: In relation to those two incidents, also we don't have direct evidence showing that Naser Oric was in command of those units. We have circumstantial evidence showing that he was indeed in effective control of these units. Naser Oric in his interview to the OTP, you can find it in -- in the second interview that he gave to the OTP, tape 2, he himself testified that for each of the attacks that were committed under his command, they would have normally three meetings. One initial meeting would be to plan. A second meeting to allocate responsibility, and a third meeting to confirm responsibilities after reconnaissance work is conducted by the respective units. Our submission, Your Honour, is that these attacks followed a similar pattern of conduct which included planning the attacks, participation in three incidents by Naser Oric, and the evaluation of the results of the attack. Your Honour, you'll see from my further submissions on the incidents of Fakovici, Bjelovac, and Kravica, in which the accused not only planned but directly participated in those attacks. In relation to the incident in Ratkovici, you will see, Your Honour, we have a combat report, P87, confirmed by witness Sead Delic, which shows that units under command of the accused did indeed participate in that attack. In relation to the attack in Jezestica, we have one witness, Miladin Simic, which confirms that the history with the head paraded by Kemo in Srebrenica relates to the events that took part -- place in the village of Jezestica. Your Honour, our submission is that this -- when this incident is confronted with the submission -- with the testimony of the witness that confirmed that Muslim, as they called, Muslim forces or forces under -- of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina have participated in that -- in that -- in those attacks, when we confront with our submissions that Naser Oric was indeed the commander of those units which participated in that attack, Your Honours could address, could see this from Exhibit P80 which was already mentioned here, it's the breakdown of the formation of -- the formation structure of the army of Srebrenica. The only reasonable conclusion is that -- that the attacks could not have been carried out without the knowledge of the commander and could not have been carried out without his control. In relation to knowledge, was the accused put in knowledge in relation to the crimes committed in those two attacks? Again, Your Honour, I would like to address you to our jurisprudence, in particular the Blaskic, and in particular to the Blaskic trial judgement and Celebici trial judgement, Kordic trial judgement, in which it was stated that when we are proving knowledge we have two aspects. The first one is knowledge which can be proven either by direct evidence or circumstantial evidence, and the second aspect is knowledge which that can be proven by providing information which was available to the accused but which he refrained not to take -- deliberately refrained not to take. Again I would like to emphasise that our case is not about vicarious liability, it's not about negligent behaviour. It's about deliberate behaviour. Information is available and the accused opts not to be acquainted with that information. In relation to circumstantial evidence, our jurisprudence is relied on the final report of the commission of expert, which stated that the following -- the following evidence can be helpful in concluding whether there was information available to the accused. The first one, the number of illegal acts. The second, the type of illegal acts. The third, the scope of illegal acts, the time during which the legal acts occurred, the number and type of troops involved, the logistics involved if any, geographical location of the acts, the widespread occurrence of the acts the tactical tempo of operations, the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: ... illegal acts, the officers and staff involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry. The location of the commander at the time. These are the type of evidence that, in combination, make -- will help Your Honours to conclude that there should have been knowledge by the accused of the acts committed. Apart from that, witnesses have testified that the village of Ratkovici was first completely looted and then burned down by forces under the control of Naser Oric. Witness Gligic, for example, has testified that the Muslim POW did confirm to him that lootings and burning were ordered by Naser Oric personally. Bogilovic and -- witness Bogilovic and Meholjic have testified that acts of looting and burning were common knowledge in Srebrenica since the population was starving. At least if Your Honours go to Exhibit number 80 -- P84, you'll see that at least once during the debriefings, the issue of the need to stop acts of wanton destruction and plunder was raised. In order from the said corps delivered by -- to Srebrenica on the 28th May 1992 is Exhibit P29. Also attested to the effect that TO units were to prohibit acts of wanton destruction and plunder. We can say that the this order again conforms to the data entered in the memo pad of the Srebrenica TO, Exhibit P84, in which the TO has requested from the 2nd Corps that they provide them the list of all the available rules that are applicable. Naser Oric himself in his interview to the OTP also has confirmed that acts of plunder and wanton destruction were taking place but again he justified it with what he called the law of survival. Again, the Defence yesterday also have conceded that these acts might have occurred but again they justified it by the justification of necessity. The Prosecution submits that where there is evidence that tends to show that forces under command of the accused have indeed participated in attack, and confirmation from witnesses and victims, that acts prohibited by the law have indeed taken place, which follow the similar pattern. That is sufficient to prove that the commander either knew from circumstantial evidence that these crimes were committed or were put on notice that such incidents might have occurred, however he preferred not to prevent or punish, justifying this attitude by necessity. The Prosecution submits that the number and type and scope of illegal acts as well as the modus operandus of similar illegal acts is indication that the accused was commander of the forces took part in the operation, was aware of the crimes, but again with this awareness he failed to either prevent or punish his subordinates. In relation to means available to the accused to prevent or punish, I would like to address it at the end because they are the same in relation to the other incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't want Mr. Wubben to start feeling alarmed that he might not have enough time to deal with number 5 because the last half hour. How much time do you think you would require to wind up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: The next group of incidents is the one that occurred in Fakovici -- the attack on Fakovici and surrounding hamlets on 5 October 1993, Bjelovac and Sikirici on 14th and 9th December 1992 -- I'm sorry, Fakovici was October 1992. These incidents are -- I put them apart because these are incidents where clear-cut Mr. Oric has participated. In relation to Fakovici, the units which participated in this attack you already know from our indictment, we put them, I only can see -- I only can say that we tendered evidence, Exhibits number P95, P84, P94, showing clearly that these were the units which participated in those attacks and were under Naser Oric at the time when the events ... Indicators of effective control in the attack on Fakovici, Naser Oric participated in plans to attack Fakovici on the 3rd October. We can see it from the memo pad, exhibit P84. Meholjic has testified about a meeting that took place before the Fakovici operation that he and Naser Oric both attended. Meholjic also states that Naser Oric was in Fakovici. Naser was present when discussing the outcome of the operation on 7 October. Again memo pad, exhibit P84. Naser Oric also has confirmed in his interview that he planned and took part in the attack on Fakovici, the second interview, tape 3 and 4. The attack was carried out is confirmed by the witness, Your Honour, who you heard it from my colleague, and P94 and P95 and the combat report, P -- Exhibit P88 confirm that the attack did indeed occur. In relation to Bjelovac, again, the list of units which participated in that attack are also from the indictment, I can only say that we tendered evidence P84, P94, P95, showing that these are the units that indeed did participate in those attacks. Which are the indicators that we have showing that the accused exercised effective control over those units? First, Naser Oric was present and offered advice on 22nd November regarding the upcoming attack on Bjelovac. He undertook to form an elite platoon. It's again from the memo pad, Exhibit P84. The accused was present at the meeting of the Srebrenica Staff on 10th December when the staff discussed the planning of attack on Bjelovac. Again, from the Exhibit P84. The accused was in charge of the combat operation during its execution. We can see it from the combat report, Exhibit number P89. The accused was present when the results of the attack on Bjelovac were discussed. Again it's from the memo pad, Exhibit P84. And again the combat report, P89, also confirms that the accused was the one responsible for the planning of the attack. We have one witness, witness Mira Stojanovic who confirmed that she saw the accused during the attack on Bjelovac. And again, in his interview the accused confirms that he planned and participated in that attack, second interview, tape 7. In relation to the attack on Kravica and Jezestica, again the units which participated in those -- in those attacks are known from the indictments. We provided, we tendered evidence showing that this was the case, and as these units were under the command of Naser Oric, Exhibit P94, P95, P84, at least, and P88. Indicators of effective control. Naser Oric was in charge of the combat operation during its execution. Exhibit P88 is a combat report. Naser Oric confirms in his interview that he participated in the planning and operation, second interview tape 9. At the meeting of the Srebrenica staff on 10 January 1993, the accused stated that the operation had been carried out well and commended all participants. It's also from the memo pad, Exhibit P84. As for the knowledge, again we have the indicators of knowledge of the crimes committed in Fakovici. We have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Aren't we repeating now, Mr. Doria, because I think you have told us all this already about twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was -- I was talking about the incidents in which we didn't have clear-cut evidence of participation of Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have been dealing with those for the last half an hour, at least. You are referring always to the same documents. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was in relation to the first incident. As I said, it was in relation to Ratkovici and -- and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you made that distinction between those two villages and others a long time ago. So let's conclude, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Yes. Now what I'm saying is, in relation to the village of Fakovici, Bjelovac, and Kravica, there is abundant evidence in the -- in the -- in the exhibits that were tendered showing that he had knowledge of those -- of the crimes committed. Again, it's the memo pad. His interview, he testifies about that. So essentially it's the memo pad and -- and -- and his interview which attests to the fact that he had knowledge of the crimes committed. As to the failure to prevent or punish, which means were available to the accused to prevent or punish? First of all, it's obvious that Naser Oric was aware that acts of looting and plunder were impermissible. We have Exhibit P29, concerning -- Exhibit P29 which was delivered to Srebrenica TO, in which specifically it's from 2nd Corps in which specifically it's stated that "acts of wanton destruction and acts of plunder are prohibited and the units should make sure that this doesn't happen." The accused himself in his interview, he say that he remembers that he also signed a document, an order, to the effect that acts of plunder and wanton destruction are prohibited. It's second -- from the second interview, tape 9. We heard witness Odzic -- Hodzic extensively talking about the means available to the accused as it relates to the laws in force that could -- that he could have used to ensure that persons under his responsibility should have either prevented or punished the particular persons who committed the crimes. Naser Oric had in his -- under his command a military police. We are not going to -- but he could have used the military police. In one instance, a military police followed orders from Srebrenica and brought individuals into custody for wilful abandoning their position. It is from Exhibit P15. Naser Oric reported a decision to form a wartime military police to the TO Staff in Tuzla, Exhibit P100. And Naser Oric has threatened to imprison individuals who refused to obey orders on mobilisation. It's Exhibit P20. Naser Oric did use the military police to bring order during the attack on Fakovici. This is from memo pad, P84. utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm much obliged and even I try to trim down my submission, in that respect that I can skip various parts in which you were already addressed. The Prosecution, there is no need to further any factual circumstances. To start, responsibility under 7(1) of the Statute, the individual responsibility is focussed on planning, instigating, ordering, committing and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. In this indictment, you have got only two kinds of 7(1) responsibility indicated, and that's instigating and aiding and abetting. Forget about the others because they are not mentioned in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, they are mentioned in the indictment and it is the Prosecution case that there is aiding and abetting and instigating, as well as I will conclude that one can construct that there is also planning and ordering. In the indictment, it has been further, the aiding and abetting, and the instigating, as well as in the pre-trial brief. It has never been the position of the Prosecution to exclude the planning and ordering. I would like to rely on the jurisprudence that where it has been established that the accused was the commander of the troops carrying out an attack, it's reasonable to infer that the accused carried out a command role during the attack. Kupreskic judgement. The requisite elements of instigating. First, that the crime was committed by a person other than the accused and actus reus is that the accused prompted, provoked, or induced the conduct of the other perpetrator. The mens rea include the intent of the crime to be committed as a result of his are provocation or inducement or anyhow an awareness of the likelihood. I will refer to the Brdjanin case in that respect and I will skip Blaskic, Galic, Strugar, and Kordic judgements, as well as corroborating that judgement. The elements of aiding and abetting as a mode of liability are that the crime was committed by a person other than the accused, and the actus reus include that the accused gave practical assistance, encouragement or moral support which had a substantial affect upon the commission of the crime. The mens rea focused on knowledge of the accused, that his conduct would substantially contribute to the commission by another person of the crime or that he was aware, again, of the substantial likelihood that this would be an adequate consequence of his conduct. I will refer to the Celebici case and as well include the Brdjanin judgement in this respect for various specifications, like there is no requirement that the accused shared the mens rea of the perpetrators. It is sufficient that he or she has knowledge that his or her actions will assist the perpetrator in the commission of the crime, and that relevant act of assistance may be removed both in time and place from the actual commission of the offences. I come to the evidence of individual responsibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You want to do it after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution incorporate at this point evidence that is previously argued this morning in the field of command responsibility of the five alleged attacks linked with wanton destruction and plunder is all in order to avoid needless reputation. To establish to the accused was not unfamiliar with the structure of command and control upon his appointment as commander in May 1992. It's important to underline his police and military career. I refer to his police background for -- in the past, as stressed in the agreed facts number 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 10, the biographical facts, and that he served in the army for several years. That means that he was familiar with the disciplining and aware of the system of command and control, the tasking, reporting, and how a hierarchy plays a role in it. He should be aware of the assistance and role of working with a Criminal Code. He should have been immersed in the culture of military and police. Naser Oric functioned also as a member of the War Presidency and participated in meetings of his staff of the TO Srebrenica. Thus, Naser Oric had vehicles for additional institutional knowledge available and the structures supported his information or position to fulfil his role as a commander of the armed forces. He was able to use both the military structure of the armed forces and the War Presidency to advance any relevant fact or circumstances related to the allegations and event you'll outcome of the attacks. This position regarding information could help him if he just wanted or choose to do so, to command and control his army, including the units. I refer to P14, the transcript of Becir Bogilovic, and the agreed facts and P84. There were also guidelines and regulations, degrees and laws available that enabled the commander to set up instructions and orders to direct the morale and behaviour of his troops. I refer to the order of the 28th May 1992 of 2nd Corps, that's the order not to burn, P29, and the commenting testimony of Sead Delic, as a witness. On the 23rd of 92, the presidency of the BiH issued an order of the adoption of rules of international laws of war by the Armed Forces of BiH coming into force on the 5th of September 1992. I refer to it. I refer to the testimony of Enver Hogic and P272. As argued earlier this morning by my colleagues, there is sufficient evidence for the crime basis of wanton destruction and plunder during and after the five alleged acts, including the three attacks that formed parts of counts 5 and 6. In addition, that evidence, all the evidence, also showed that the accused was the commander of the units participating in these attacks. The overall commander. These units committed the attacks including the wanton destruction and plunder. There are acts and omissions by the accused that constitute an actus reus of instigating and aiding and abetting. There was no disciplining during the attacks regarding preventing the burning and looting. Naser Oric failed to take reasonable measures thereof. He didn't make use of seeking the support of the command line via Tuzla or Sarajevo to address that problem and request adequate assistance. In the report sent to Tuzla and Sarajevo, they show during the course of the trial there is no -- not a reference to such a request for advice or assistance to maintain discipline or to take the appropriate measures. And indeed there were in Srebrenica problems regarding discipline. I refer to Hakija Meholjic as a witness. While at the same time, Naser Oric considered himself subordinated to Tuzla and Sarajevo, he failed to ask for any assistance or seek for any measures to support him in that respect. I will refer to the reports that show that he was able to address his superiors with reporting regarding the attacks but do not refer to any problems in that regard, meaning P279, D -- P100, there are reports signed the 2nd of July 1992, also refer to in the interview accused and the transcript testimony Ibrahim Becirevic when it comes to communication and information service, with no mentioning of need for help to monitor and discipline behaviour of soldiers regardless the events in Ratkovici and later the other events during other attacks. This failure of -- can be concluded from the opinion from accused regarding his role as a commander of the armed forces under his command,. That opinion include a focus on leadership of leading combat actions and other combat role that include monitoring of behaviour regarding war crimes such as burning and looting. He stated by himself that he was responsible for the situation in the field, not being interested in any paperwork. I refer to his interview in that respect. There is no follow-up of the order of the 28th of May 1992, and the decree by the president regarding the application of international laws of war, and I quote him, "We had to defend ourselves with all means available, that means by observing and not observing the Geneva Conventions, both the Serbian and the Muslim side." I also note the labelling of the fact of the Muslim side. And I quote, "It was necessary to fully respect the Geneva Conventions, and I think that the command corps did not change its position from the very beginning and right up until the end of the war." I apologise, that is not the quotation of the accused, Your Honours. It's the transcript testimony of Hogic, and I refer to it. However, accused underlined another opinion in that respect. "I'm not a commander that knew all of the Geneva Conventions." There was, however, for him available a training centre in Tuzla and he didn't make use of it. I refer to Delic testimony in that respect. He signed a report dated the 3rd of July, that's P100, 3rd of July 1992, of the Srebrenica TO as a commander. This report was addressed to the Sarajevo Republican Staff and the staff in Tuzla. He reported again on results regarding an attack avoiding, not mentioning the need for the assistance, as I alleged earlier. Important to note is that there was an existence of a pool of former reserve officers available for Naser Oric. In his interview he clarified that it was Ramiz, that is Ramiz Becirovic, task to think of plan together with other former officers of the JNA. I explicitly refer to his interview in that respect. So this Ramiz could collect a group of these former reserve officers, among them Hamid Salihovic, former reserve officer of the military security. So are also named Ferid, Hodzic, as a person who is -- who has this former military expertise. With respect to the mens rea, I will refer to the fact that apparently there it was a leak about any action to follow in regard to a projected attack. Meholjic, witness Meholjic confirmed that at a meeting about Fakovici, Witness Meholjic said that there had been a leak about the action. "The people followed us. The people started even before us. Everybody knew when the action took place. There was a leak every time, before every action. Naser Oric should be aware of it. He was aware at several meetings, 3rd of October, 7th of October, when this collection of goods and plundering has been addressed." That's Exhibit P84. In his interview he confirmed that what happened in the village he found out afterwards. He also confirmed that it was the same practice in all Territorial Defence units to bring down a lot of unarmed people to carry out wounded and material and supplies, supplies, Your Honour. "You can take what you can get, whatever you can grab, that's yours. And everybody takes that home to his own house or to his own unit." End quotation of his interview. There was an intent to share the practice, to plunder or to burn down property, and he had an -- he, the accused, had a passive attitude when confronted with crimes. When -- when he was confronted with a demonstration of resignation as early discussed related to document P255, it's a resignation by members of the Srebrenica Staff, there was a meeting called by the accused. I refer to that document P14, P84, as the minutes of that meeting. In the minutes, from the minutes, it is clear that Naser Oric was present, and he opened the meeting, read the decision out, leaving the OS Staff and the letter of resignation was subject of discussion at the meeting. It's important to refer to that letter of resignation as he as a commander was put on notice that the writers of the letter prefer not to burn in their consciences that the liberation of new areas from occupation only increases crime and the destruction of private and socially owned property, and apparently there was no follow-up. Not during the discussion at that meeting, nor later on. And I refer to the fact that the Kravica attack has to be planned and was about to project from that date on. Naser Oric stated in his interview and reply to a question whether the soldiers as well were taking things and running back to the family, he replied, "Everybody did that." And also I refer to the meeting of the staff of the TO Srebrenica of the 10th of January, after the Kravica attack. Naser Oric is quoted in the minutes stating that the operation has been carried out well and that he commended all participants. The alleged behaviour and discipline of the soldiers during and after the Kravica area attack did apparently not form part of any measures or measures discussed or a general discussion triggered by Naser Oric as the overall command. When it comes, Your Honour, please give me some guidance how many minutes are left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have -- Mr. Jones, 15 or 20?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think more like 20 minutes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Twenty. So you have 12 more minutes or 13 more minutes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I can finalise, Your Honour. I come to the part of ordering and planning. In the indictment the accused is alleged also to be liable in the modus of ordering and planning of the crimes of plunder and wanton destruction as mentioned in counts 5 and 6. The acts and omissions previously submitted by me in the field of instigating and aiding and abetting, but it can also be adduced in the field of individual responsibility, ex Article 7(1) for planning and ordering such war crimes. The plan -- the elements of planning are one or several persons contemplate designing the commission of a crime at both preparatory and execution phases. It is sufficient to demonstrate that the planning was a factor of substantially contributing to such criminal conduct, its actus reus, and the accused directly or indirectly intended the crime in question to be committed. A person who plans an act or commission with the awareness of the substantial likelihood that the crime will be committed in execution of that plan has the requisite mens rea for establishing this responsibility under Article 7(1). Planning with such an awareness has to be regarding as accepting the crime. I refer to the jurisprudence, the Brdjanin judgement, as well as the Kordic and Cerkic judgement. It's not the judgement. It's the Appeals Chamber decision of the 17th of December. The requisite elements of ordering are that first, a person in a position of authority uses that authority to instruct another to commit an offence or give an explicit order. It's not necessary to demonstrate the existence of a formal superior-subordinate relationship between the accused and the perpetrator. An order should be implied. Causal link between the act of ordering and the physical perpetration of a crime, that order does not need to be given in any particular form, nor does it have to be given by the person in position of authority directly to the person committing the offence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to read slower? It is too fast for the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I apologise. The existence of an order may be proven through direct or circumstantial evidence. The person ordering, third, must be aware, so mens rea, of the substantial likelihood that the crime committed would be a consequence of the implementation of the order. Again, I refer to the Brdjanin, the Strugar judgement, as well. The additional evidence constituting ordering and planning of the alleged crimes under counts 5 and 6, from the command responsibility evidence material as well as the evidence material already adduced by me, it is possible to identify a basis for evidence for -- of ordering and planning the crimes as alleged under 5 and 6. There is sufficient evidence that the accused as a commander was involved in the planning and ordering of the attacks and, Your Honours, of course, I make the distinction of ordering and planning an attack and ordering and planning of a crime. But it is very important to be aware of the fact that in around this -- such attacks, these crimes, plundering and wanton destruction, occurs. The evidence already demonstrated the relevant circumstances of the overall commandership of Naser Oric and organising and implementation of the decision of the attacks and of his overall command. Will you bear me one moment, please, Your Honour? With a view to the Fakovici attack, I refer to the transcript testimony of Hakija Meholjic in which he confirmed that Zulfo Tursunovic and Naser Oric organised that attack. A meeting took place before the Fakovici operation regarding the attack, that Meholjic and Naser Oric both attended. I refer to the transcript, the memo pad, page 3 and 4, and his interview regarding Fakovici, the interview of the accused. Naser Oric was personally present at Fakovici, confirmed by Hakija Meholjic. I refer to the transcript regarding Bjelovac, I refer to the interview of accused, regarding Bjelovac, tape 21, page 23, in video 2920, also the memo pad, P84, page 26, 27, I cite the testimony of Hakija Meholjic. Naser Oric planned this attack on Bjelovac, and I refer also to the action combat report, P89, and the testimony of Sead Delic. The Kravica attack --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, you seem to be -- to continue labouring on planning and ordering when I have already told you what our view is, that it -- in other words, you're seeing them in the indictment where they are obviously missing, and you are going to end up missing completely your submissions on instigating and aiding and abetting, which are the ones we really want to hear submissions about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I -- my submission include ordering and planning, and this also corroborate the aiding and abetting, so meaning that when I finalise this, then it's the finalising also of the evidence named in both -- in all forms of and modes of liability ex Article 7(1). And in the Kravica attack, I refer to the testimony of Hakija Meholjic, and that accused admitted to have played a role in Kravica standing in front of the troop. Beside that, Naser Oric also made remark with a view to his behaviour in attacks in general. Quoting him, "I was always the one with the gun in the hand going in front of the troop. I was always the one leading, as far as the Chetniks is concerned. So I was taking part as much as possible and always I am leading." Refer to the interview of the accused, and also a part in which he speaks about the planning in general of attacks. In a general manner, Naser Oric clarified that planning for the attacks took place over several days. We had this one meeting where we gave off -- where we gave all of those tasks. The second meeting was to allocate this -- the directions of attack, and then the third meeting would come afterwards, after everybody would have received their directions of attacks, they would then go out and carry out reconnaissance from where they were supposed to be. We would then have a meeting again. I refer to the interview. This evidence, Your Honours, will also assist in the evidence of instigating and abetting, and so vice versa, and as this is an area regarding preparing an offensive and in which he was able to address the morale, the behaviour, and to anticipate any instructions thereof. Within the scope of evidence for planning and ordering, it's in an approach of accentuating the knowledge that accused had, whenever the planning started, and the decision or order for the military offensive action had to be executed by the forces. There was a substantial likelihood of burning and looting, as shown in the evidence already submitted. After experiencing the attacks by troops under his command, from as early as June 1992, and the fact of burning and looting that took place ever since, during or shortly after these attacks, is an indirect attempt to accept such practice as a predictable outcome, being a self-filling part of planning or ordering attacks even if such a burning or looting is not explicitly included in that planning and ordering. By planning and ordering the attacks on Fakovici, Bjelovac, and Kravica area, together with Jezestica, Naser Oric was aware or should be aware of the substantially likelihood of burning and looting, meaning that at any rate with the ordering and planning of the attack there is an implicit planning and order for war crimes of unlawful burning and looting in the area of the projected offensive at the planned time. This -- Naser Oric, by organising the attacks, he also accepted, according to jurisprudence an indirect intent, the planning, ordering of the burning down of houses and plunder of private property belonging to the population of the Serbian ethnicity of the villages -- in the villages in the area of Fakovici, Bjelovac, and Kravica. I conclude my argument for individual responsibility 7(1) by accused taking into account the evidence as produced. I conclude that there is evidence capable of supporting a conviction of accused Naser Oric being individually responsible under Article 7(1) of the Statute. Your Honour, I arrive for a half minute with the concluding remarks, chapter six. This morning, and the beginning this afternoon, my co-counsels and I have submitted and concluded that there is sufficient or better capable evidence to support a conviction of Naser Oric for the crimes as alleged in counts 1 to 6 of the indictment. The indictment should stand and accordingly, there is a case to answer. Therefore, the Prosecution respectfully requests that the Trial Chamber proceed with the case against Naser Oric to final judgement. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Mr. Jones, I take it that you would like -- yes, one moment. Judge Eser would -- to whom? Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, just for the reason to clarify, in which paragraph of the indictment would you find or could the Trial Chamber find that Naser Oric is accused of planning and ordering?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's in the beginning of the indictment, Your Honours, where it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: If I may assist you, there is reference to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yeah. It's paragraph 12, Your Honour. "Individual criminal responsibility includes planning, instigating, ordering, committing, or otherwise aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation, or executions of any acts or omissions set forth in this indictment." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. If I might start with that last point, and draw attention to a -- what's now Prosecution Exhibit, and it was the correspondence between the parties relating to agreed facts, et cetera. At paragraph -- paragraph 6 of our issue outline, it's the issue outline dated 12th November 2003, quite a considerable time ago, we wrote in relation to -- we wrote to the Prosecution and in relation to Article 7(1) we wrote, "We affirm our understanding based on the issue outline in paragraph 38 of the amended indictment that the Prosecution is basing the alleged responsibility of Naser Oric, the accused, under Article 7(1) of the ICTY Statute exclusively on allegations of instigating and aiding and abetting offences within the injuries particulars of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to read slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we never received anything from the Prosecution to indicate that that understanding was incorrect and we've proceeded during this trial on the basis that it was merely instigating and aiding and abetting which were charged, and in our pre-trial brief when we set out the elements for Article 7(1) liability, again we dealt with instigating and aiding and abetting. I may come back to that but that's always been our understanding, and we would have major issues if the Prosecution were to change tack now. Now I'll respond in a very brief time I have to some of the points raised by the Prosecution. And, of course, given the time, I can't respond to all the points. In sum, I say nothing you've heard today shakes our submissions from yesterday. The summary of the evidence which has been presented by the Prosecution is in fact been full of inaccuracies, I have to say, and I'll take you to specific chapter and verse. I have half a dozen examples which I've noted already. The interview of our client has been completely misrepresented in many respects and Your Honours will of course -- I understand Your Honour also of course be reading or have read the interview in its entirety and I suspect that's all the more necessary now that bits and pieces of the interview have been taken out, out of their context and, we would say, misrepresented. P84 has been referred to a great deal and again we would say completely misrepresented in parts. Just to give one example, Mr. Di Fazio referred to 49 burnt villages which, clear from the context, that context, that refers to Muslim villages, burnt Muslim villages, in the Skelani area. And again, the Prosecution there would have you believe that these were Serb villages and that's the sort of gross distortion of P84 which is, in our submission, unacceptable and which will have to be corrected at least at some stage and if I may note in that regard there was a witness, Prosecution witness, potential witness, Mustafa Salihovic, who was actually the note taker of P84 and who would have been someone who'd have been in a position to actually help Your Honours in how to interpret P84 and what was meant and what was -- and what the context was. He was dropped. The Prosecution would prefer you not to have the full picture of what was actually going on in these meetings and simply take words out of context and get to a conviction, ultimately, I imagine that way. So the essence of what I'll be saying in this brief period now is that the Prosecution should in a Rule 98 bis submission at least get the evidence right. They have the transcripts. There is therefore no excuse for misstating what the evidence was. Before I come to a couple of those examples, I also want to say by way of general remark, that some of what we heard from the Prosecution is just sheer fantasy. And I'll take one example, that Naser Oric should have attended a training centre in Tuzla, that he should have crawled through 100 kilometres of enemy lines, minefields, risked his life to attend a training in Tuzla. And the reason I mention that which strikes me, and I think anyone of common sense, as so absurd is that you have to trust the judgement of the Prosecution in a lot of these matters when they express disapproval of Naser Oric or if they criticise his failings. I mean, if this is a Prosecution who thinks that a person is obliged to crawl through enemy lines to attend a training I say you have to shall very sceptical about their judgement. Now, killings, if I can deal with that firstly, Prosecution has only dealt with knowledge in relation to the killing of Mr. Kukic. And not with the six others or now five others. As regards what the evidence was about the killing by Kemo, I want to make clear that our concession is that that was the evidence given by Radic. We are certainly not conceding the truth of any of those matters. Our concession is that was evidence which was given. But the Prosecution hasn't provided you with any information regarding knowledge of the five other killings and if I pose the question, why not? I'd answer it's because there is no evidence that Naser Oric knew of these five other killings and so I'd certainly invite Your Honours in light of that implicit concession to stop the case regarding these other murders because -- or what's charged as murders, because there is no evidence of knowledge on Naser Oric's part and knowing about beatings cannot be the same thing as knowing about killings, otherwise every cruel treatment under 7(3) would implicitly -- would implicitly carry with it a conviction for murder under Article 7(3). That cannot be right. There must be more and the Prosecution hasn't even addressed what more there is. Now, as far as the presentation of killings, of the evidence in relation to beatings and killings was concerned, there were some major inaccuracies which Ms. Richardson put before you, and I'll take one example. She made a great play of the fact that Ilija Ivanovic was prone, was lying on the floor in front of the person alleged to be Naser Oric. That was something which I went to great pains in cross-examination to make clear, because it's obviously a mistake. And I'll read from the transcript, 26 of January 2005. And I put to him: "Leaving that meeting aside I want to clarify one point about the meeting in the reception room if you can go back to that, and I believe there may have been a misunderstanding. You seem to be telling us that when you were brought into the reception room with the five or so people you were lying down in front of the people. Now is that correct? Or were you in fact standing up when you saw them?" Answer: "That's not correct. I never said that. Nobody forced us to lie down on the floor. We were standing in front of them, and they were deliberating amongst themselves, asking some questions. I never said that we were prone. I simply said that we were lying down when we were being beating. That's all." That's was his Andja. How much clearer can he be, and how can it be right to still suggest to Your Honours that they were lying prone in this reception room? Ms. Richardson said that Mrki was in uniform. Andjelko Radic on the 13th of January said, "Three occasions Mrki was wearing civilian clothes. I didn't see him in uniform. He was a civilian."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, if there is one person who said Mrki was in uniform and three who said that he never was in uniform, that's for the final judgement, not for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm saying that the evidence was misstated in relation to what was said about Mrki. It was suggested that there was a positive identification by Ilija Ivanovic of Naser Oric. Again, I'm looking at the transcript of the 26th of January 2005. "Today, sitting there where you are, you can't say for sure can you whether you ever laid eyes on Naser Oric in the reception room in the prison." Answer: "I've said this, haven't I. I really didn't know him. I've confirmed a number of times that I didn't see him." And he said, other things on that subject, to the effect that -- I asked him whether he was sure of seeing Oric in the room. He answered: "I fully understand what you mean. As I've said, I don't know him personally. I don't know if he was there, but I think I've explained with sufficient clarity what my assumption was based on. But I did say a number of times I simply don't know -- didn't know whether it was him or not." Furthermore, it was suggested or said that the evidence showed that Serbs said they were interviewed by Hamid Salihovic. That's the Prosecution's inference matching together documents with testimony. No detainee gave evidence that he was interviewed by Hamid Salihovic. You referred to the interview with Naser Oric where allegedly he said that he knew that Zulfo was visiting the prisoners. Again that's not correct. It was in the context of trying to establish a military court that Naser Oric made remarks about Zulfo's familiarity with the prison system and the judicial system because of his time in prison. So I say all that to make clear that Your Honours will have to review very carefully what the Prosecution has said today about the evidence. We provided slides and references to every quotation we proceeded and you can check. But as for these summaries, they really are not accurate for the most part. Now, Your Honours know what Hakija said about Kemo and all the "I don't knows" with which he spoke of any affiliation that Kemo might have had. His evidence was linked immediately with P80 which Hakija said bore no resemblance to reality. I'm not going to make submissions on documents, but the Prosecution surely can't pick and choose one thing that Hakija said and then ignore what he said in the next breath. The OTP would have you ignore all that and have you take Hakija's evidence that Kemo was at the relevant time at the time of the killing a soldier in the Pale battalion. And that's quite simply not Hakija Meholjic's evidence. You know what the evidence regarding Sarac was as well. I won't say the evidence of Sarac, because he didn't give evidence. He wasn't available for cross-examination, and a we know what Mr. Radic said about the inaccuracy of what Sarac said when being interviewed. You know that there was never positive identification of Oric in the sense that there was not a single photo, identification procedure, or an identity parade carried out in this case. You know that Nedjeljko Radic spoke of the Oric which he saw as being -- having a height of 167 -- 160 centimetres, blue eyes, and being clean shaven, whereas the Prosecution evidence, and this is the Prosecution's evidence because it says Major Mujkanovic among others, 180 centimetres, brown eyes, bearded, and if that's a positive identification, then a certain expression involving monkeys and uncles comes to mind. It's also misstated that Naser Oric went in and took a prisoner out of the PTT building. That was the summary which Ms. Richardson provided. It's at page 29, line 4, today that was not Colonel Tucker's evidence. Again, these are important matters where accuracy counts for everything, and surely on the 98 bis submission the Prosecution at least have to get the evidence right. I'll move on to question of plunder and wanton destruction. Now, Mr. Di Fazio spoke rather picturesquely of hillside villages and peasants living in some sort of rustic innocence and then merely being attacked. But look at P88 and P89 which have been referred to, and what was seized from those villages in terms of military hardware. The forms themselves speak of military necessity in terms of the tactical and strategic operation or necessity of the actions of what was seized from the enemy forces. And again, this -- I'll come back to this repeatedly, the Prosecution are ignoring in effect the evidence of the insiders. Now, they called Dr. Mujkanovic, Hakija Meholjic, Becir Bogilovic, maybe they don't like the evidence which they gave, but that is Prosecution evidence, and taking the Prosecution evidence as its highest doesn't mean ignoring everything which is inconvenient or which doesn't fit. He said that every raid was necessary for food and ammunition. And the destruction was an unfortunate by-product done by civilians. Again, Mr. Di Fazio said that all the Prosecution evidence was of village guards simply minding their own business. Again, all the Prosecution evidence, if you ignore what the insiders said, if you ignore what Dr. Gow testified about what was happening in the region, if you ignore what the insiders said about how much of a military presence was in the area, how there were Serb artillery which was shelling them every day. But that -- 98 bis doesn't entitle one to just simply ignore all of that evidence. Mr. Di Fazio said that there wasn't any evidence ever of people being attacked in trenches first. Well, that's not true. In Jezestica there was evidence of people in trenches being attacked and of heavy weaponry being seized at the beginning of the action. And when we look at plunder, it is important to consider the items which the Prosecution say were taken. Because if they are saying, Oh, well we are not concerned with food, food is completely out of the picture, then they may have to drop cattle from the indictment because it certainly is a fact, especially among starving people, that if they take cattle, it's a good chance they are going to kill the cattle and eat them. If it's merely a question of TV sets and furniture, then that's when inventory does become important, and we will certainly be going back and looking in each action what was the evidence that furniture and TV sets were stolen? I think you'll find it's very minimal. The -- and in addition I might just say as an aside that the Prosecution nonetheless did continue to deal with the notion of food and the suggestion that it's not the lesser evil to take food from the Serbs because then they would starve. That just ignores the whole context that the Serbs weren't under siege, the Bosniaks in Srebrenica were under siege, and that the Serbs had all of Serbia and kilometres of their territory behind them, and I don't think there has been a single piece of evidence that a Serb ever starved as a result of having his property taken by people who were under siege. And I come to this argument of Mr. Di Fazio, that furniture -- because furniture is a household possession, that if evidence is given of household possessions being taken then it must include furniture. Well, that's a complete logical fallacy. It's of a nature of the logical fallacy that if a cat is a mammal; therefore, if it's a mammal it must be a cat. It simply does not follow. It could be kettles, lamps, any of the thousand of household items which were not furniture which were taken and never mind the fallacy in logic of saying that if furniture is a household item, if a household item is taken it must be an item of furniture. Clear fallacy. The fact this furniture is heavy, if anything else, sofas and chairs, and perhaps old ladies, and civilians, can take household items, but not furniture. Anyway, it would be a complete fallacy to say that any reference to household possession must include furniture. It's the fallacy of affirming the consequent, if one has studied logic. But again in all of this the key issue has not been addressed, that -- how is one to say this these people carrying out these acts of plunder were subordinates of Oric? Mr. Di Fazio seemed to suggest that you can just fasten on this, the magic use of the word soldiers by a Serb and then be satisfied that that's sufficient evidence that these were soldiers in organised units. Often, in fact, the term "soldier" was suggested to witnesses in examination-in-chief but beyond that, the evidence, the Prosecution evidence, has been that it was impossible to distinguish between civilians and fighters, although Mr. Di Fazio would ask you to ignore that and not consider how a Serb actually would know who is a fighter and who is not. I would refer to something which Your Honour said at one stage when this whole matter came up. It was when I objected to the Prosecution leading by asking whether people were soldiers, saying that it calls for a judgement on the part of the witness. And Ms. Richardson said, I think every time we go through these questions about the person wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, it's just that I'm short of time. "I think every statement we go through these questions about the person wearing the uniform it's redundant. And I think at the end of the day Your Honours are able to judge for yourself whether the description, the characterisation of the person being described is a soldier or not." And Your Honour said: "I can assure you we will be in that position." Your Honours are in that position. You are going to have to decide whether someone it was a fighter or a civilian. It's not enough just to trust that Milenko Stevanovic, when he says "soldier" is referring to a fighter in an organised unit. The fact is, as emerged from the evidence, that in fact Serbs had all sorts of different definitions of what was a soldier, whether it was just a young man with a weapon or someone in a bit of uniform, and the consistent evidence is that way -- that's why ribbons were needed precisely because there was no way to distinguish by sight alone. And again, only by ignoring all of the insiders' evidence could you arrive at the conclusion that this is satisfactory evidence that there were soldiers involved. And then review of the actions has been incredibly selective. It's been a question of looking at one house here, one house there, and that's why I referred to a notion of an inventory because, in fact, what our client is entitled to and what Your Honour is entitled to is a demonstration that this was the damage caused in this action and this witness saw these people committing that damage or that plunder, and those people are now shown by some evidence to be a subordinate of Naser Oric and it's shown that he knew that his subordinates will committed those crimes. There is a -- discrete links which need to be shown in a proper criminal case. Instead the Prosecution is inviting you to a broad-brush approach to see some fighters here, some destruction there, a bit of what Mira Filipovic saw, a bit of what someone else said, and arrive at the conclusion that this is all satisfactory demonstration of command responsibility for these crimes. It isn't. In fact for Mira Filipovic - she admitted it, in fact - she didn't see her house burnt down. It could have been an empty menace. She saw it was -- the house was burnt next day, I think that's what Mr. Di Fazio said. I'm going to have to check all these references now. But the fact is someone else could have done it in the meantime. Fighters, civilians, displaced persons. We haven't made any -- in fact, the Prosecution hasn't answered the questions which I put yesterday. Finally a few matters on -- if I may, may I be permitted five minutes, Your Honour? I know we are running over, or do we have until 2.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we don't have until 2.00. We have until quarter to 2.00, and I have a bureau meeting soon after this sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll try to make my last points in a very quick way. The Prosecution has added glosses to certain exhibits, P84. Mr. Di Fazio referred to Oric's inner circle and no witness ever said that the people at that meeting were Oric's inner circle. He's not summarising evidence, he's spinning it. I've referred to the reference to burning down 42 villages and the suggestion those were Serb villages. Again, all matters which Your Honours will have to look at very carefully and not simply rely on the summary which has been provided today. The Prosecution has totally ignored the issue of the independence of Hakija's unit, Zulfo's unit, Akif's unit. They are inviting you to consider that Naser Oric was the overall commander of all forces in spite of their own evidence. And again I pose the question: How for any of the crimes can they be sure that they weren't committed by fighters who were independent of Oric? Mr. Doria summarised the evidence in relation to the actions incorrectly when he said that the combat action sheet for I think it's P87 was for Ratkovici. It's for Ducice on the 19th of June, and the action sheet says it started and ended on that day. Well, is that just a mistake or are the Prosecution really going to give such a vague presentation that they'll say, Well, you can consider that Ducice on the 19th is more or less the same thing as Ratkovici on the 21st. I really hope not. Your Honours, on Article 7(1), I would just say that our understanding has been very clear from the beginning that we haven't had to deal with aiding and abetting, and instigating, and you'll see in my question to Dr. Mujkanovic, I asked whether Oric aided and abetted or instigated those crimes. I didn't -- we haven't in the whole trial gone into ordering and planning because we didn't believe we were called upon to address that. And so if Prosecution changes their position now, we reserve the right to make some pretty strong protestations. Finally, two last matters. In summarising the background of the client it was fairly typical, I think, of the Prosecution to say that Naser Oric served in the army for several years, he did his compulsory JNA military service. But again it's an instance of selective presentation, ignoring inconvenient facts, glossing over anything which goes against their theory rather than presenting their case fairly and fully, which makes Your Honours' task all the more difficult. Finally, I would just say that the Prosecution's presentation today has not been a systematic review. I said in my opening speech that you would only be presented a partial picture. To give another metaphor, the Prosecution are presenting you with bits of a jigsaw, and in fact they are different jigsaw puzzles and they're trying to hammer together pieces of different jigsaws which simply don't fit. In a proper case, these pieces would fit. But they don't unless you bang them into places where they don't belong. You have the picture, I trust, at the close of the Prosecution case, the true picture given by the insiders and the others. That picture speaks for itself which is that this case should not continue. Finally, I would ask that if Your Honours do dismiss the case in full, please do so in writing because otherwise it might be ultra vires Article 23.2 of the Statute which requires written judgement. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That brings the submissions to an end. We will hand down our oral decision on Wednesday, the 8th of June. Have we managed to transfer the sitting -- the hearing to the morning? We have. All right. So that will be at 9.00 in the morning or at any other time during that morning that will be notified to you should we change the 9.00. Thank you.
